item.title: [UPDATED] 2027: Don’t Worry About Purveyors Of Violence, There Will Be Peaceful Elections, Tinubu Tells Voters
item.description: Amid growing concerns over electoral violence in some parts of the country, President Bola Tinubu has assured Nigerians that the 2027 general elections will be peaceful. ﻿ Tinubu, who is seeking re-election on the platform of the All Progressives Congress (APC), gave the assurance while speaking at the North-Central presidential campaign rally in Jos, Plateau State, on Saturday, urging the electorate to exercise their right by voting with their permanent voter card. “That’s your weapon to prosperity; that’s your roadmap. Use it effectively well. Use it to vote APC,” he said. “Don’t worry about vagabonds. Don’t worry about purveyors of violence. We will take care of you. There will be peaceful elections. Go out and vote; vote for the candidates of the APC.” ‘Forgive Me’ While recalling his last visit to the state to meet with victims of attacks, the President asked families affected by the deadly attacks in Anguwan Rukuba , in Jos North Local Government Area of the state that left many killed and several injured to forgive him for not visiting the communities. “When I last visited the other time, I was limited to the airport. Forgive me if you didn’t see me in the hinterland. But I saw the devastation; I got the report from the governor. I saw horror in the faces of our people. “But since then, that has changed; we are forging together. He, however, assured residents that their communities would be rebuilt for those displaced to return home. Tinubu said too many lives had been lost to attacks in Plateau since 2001. He condoled with families who have lost loved ones to such attacks. Calling for unity, the President said speaking different languages should not lead to divisions. “I have directed all the security agencies to take decisive action and sustain peace and stability on the Plateau. “What we should be getting is prosperity, not havoc, not crisis. Our government is not elected to inflict wounds on one another or to bury people. We have to lift people up from penury to prosperity. “One thousand forest guards are undergoing training right now. You will feel them; you will see them. You will feel secure in your villages and communities,” he added. The President also said the surveillance cameras had been procured as promised. He warned that his administration would not tolerate violence as campaigns gather momentum ahead of the 2027 general elections. item.title: Why did Starship Flight 15 booster abort 'chopsticks' landing catch? SpaceX still investigating (video)
item.description:
Tariq is the Editor-in-Chief of Space.com based out of our New York City office and joined the team in 2001, first as an intern and staff writer, and later as an editor. He covers human spaceflight, exploration and space science, as well as skywatching and entertainment. He became Space.com's Managing Editor in 2009 and Editor-in-Chief in 2019. In October 2022, Tariq received the Harry Kolcum Award for excellence in space reporting from the National Space Club Florida Committee. In June 2025, the National Space Society awarded him the Space Pioneer Award for Excellence in Mass Media at the International Space Development Conference in Orlando, Florida.

Hailing from Stockton, California (where he attended the same high school as NASA astronaut Jose Hernandez), Tariq studied print journalism and astronomy at the University of Southern California in Los Angeles, earning a bachelor's degree in journalism in 1999 along with a minor in astronomy. He then served as a staff reporter for The Los Angeles Times covering education and city beats in La Habra and Fullerton in Orange County for the Our Times sections.

In 2000, Tariq became the city reporter for the Huntington Beach Independent, a weekly publication of the Los Angeles Times, covering local politics and events, crime, business and environmental issues. He left the Los Angeles Times in 2001 to study science journalism at New York University, where he earned a master's degree in 2002 from NYU's Science and Environmental Reporting Program (now the Science, Health and Environmental Reporting Program) under the direction of space reporter William Burrows.

Tariq first joined Space.com as an intern in September 2001 while also serving as a research assistant for nutrition writer Gary Taubes and writing freelance projects, where his work appeared in The Scientist and Laboratory Equipment Magazine. He became a full-time reporter covering spaceflight in 2004, with this first launch being NASA's STS-114 Return to Flight mission in July 2005.

Tariq is also an Eagle Scout (yes, he has the Space Exploration merit badge) and went to Space Camp four times as a kid and a fifth time as an adult. When not writing about space, you can find Tariq watching the latest Star Trek TV series, sci-fi movies and reading about hippos, his favorite animal. You can find Tariq at Space.com and as the co-host to the This Week In Space podcast with space historian Rod Pyle on the TWiT network. To see his latest project, you can follow Tariq on Twitter @tariqjmalik.

SpaceX is looking into why its latest Starship megarocket test flight missed the first of two planned landings on Friday (Nov. 13), triggering an automatic abort that destroyed the booster. The giant Starship rocket , a massive two-stage vehicle that's the largest launcher on Earth, soared into orbit from SpaceX's Starbase in South Texas on Friday on the company's ambitious Flight 15 test flight. The goal: To land both the Super Heavy first stage and the Ship upper stage, for the first full Starship recovery — and the first complete recovery of an orbital launch system in history. The Super Heavy stage, called Booster 22, came back to Earth mere minutes after liftoff as planned. Instead of returning to its launch tower to be caught mid-air by the tower's metal "chopstick" arms , however, the rocket veered offshore and detonated its flight termination system. SpaceX spokesperson Dan Huot initially said that a guidance issue appeared to be the cause. The Super Heavy first-stage booster of SpaceX's Starship Flight 15 rocket explodes during splashdown in the Gulf of Mexico after launching its Ship upper stage to orbit from Starbase, Texas on Nov. 13, 2026. (Image credit: Josh Dinner, Space.com/Future) Starship Die Cast Rocket Model Was $47.99 Now $39.99 on Amazon . Even if you can't see SpaceX's Starship in person, you can score a model of your own. Standing at 13.77 inches (35 cm), this is a 1:375 ratio of SpaceX's Starship as a desktop model. The materials here are alloy steel and it weighs just 225g. View Deal "We were initially 'go' for a catch," Huot said during live commentary on Friday, about seven hours into the mission. "But in the later stages of the coast, the booster aborted itself for a GNC issue that it detected, and that put it into its contingency landing offshore." Super Heavy exploded a few feet above the waves of the Gulf of Mexico about 6.5 minutes after liftoff. GNC is short for Guidance and Navigation Control, a criticial system used by rockets to control their flight and ensure they remain on their planned course. Such a system is vital for any landing attempt by a Starship Super Heavy or Ship upper stage to ensure the vehicle returns to its landing site safely and doesn't veer off course to damage SpaceX's Starbase or surrounding populated areas. In an update during SpaceX's Flight 15 coverage on Saturday, however, Huot said that Super Heavy's GNC system actually performed well. "I did a disservice to our booster GNC guys last night," Huot said. "It was not a GNC issue that caused us not to come back. GNC triggered that abort; it was doing what it was supposed to do. Basically, [it] detected that the booster was not in the place that it was supposed to be to proceed with a catch, did an automated abort and then headed out to that offshore splashdown location." SpaceX is "still digging into the root cause on how we got there, and so, more to come on that," he added on Saturday. You can follow our Starship Flight 15 live updates for the latest on the mission. SpaceX's Starship Flight 15 Super Heavy Booster's explosive offshore landing abort in pictures. (Image credit: Josh Dinner/Steve Spaleta/Space.com/Future) Super Heavy is powered by a cluster of 33 Raptor rocket engines that fire simultaneously during liftoff to send the 41-story Starship megarocket into orbit. During Friday's launch, all 33 engines fired as planned for the ascent, Huot said. One engine did drop out after stage separation, when Super Heavy dropped away from Ship and flipped over for a "boostback" burn to begin its trip back to Earth, Huot said on Friday. "We had 32 out of the 33 booster engines lit for boostback, which started sending it back here to the launch site," he added. A close look at the 33 Raptor engines firing simultaneously to launch SpaceX's Starship Flight 15 mission into orbit. (Image credit: Josh Dinner, Space.com/Future) That firing was followed by the booster's landing burn. In SpaceX's launch video , Super Heavy can be seen activating 13 of its Raptor engines as planned, followed by the abort and the booster steering itself to a contingency landing zone in Gulf waters. "It did that hover, cut the engines off, the FTS — the flight termination system — triggered, and it splashed down in the water," Huot said on Friday. (The FTS is designed to destroy a booster in the event of an emergency.) As its name suggests, Starship Flight 15 is SpaceX's 15th test flight of the giant rocket, but it will be the first to attempt to catch a Ship upper stage with the chopsticks. SpaceX has successfully caught Super Heavy boosters on three test flights to date. Flight 15's Ship vehicle is in good health and will orbit Earth a total of 14 times before landing back at its launch pad in Starbase at around 4:20 p.m. EST (1920 GMT) today, if all goes well. "Our heat shield team reviewed all the data we got from our ground-tracking cameras, and from those satellite cameras and confirmed the heat shield is in a good posture for a reentry and return to the launch site," Huot said in Friday's mission update. (Flight 15 hauled 26 of SpaceX's next-gen Starlink V3 satellites to orbit, and a few of those spacecraft carried cameras for heat-shield ins

item.title: On this day in space! Nov. 14, 1969: NASA's Apollo 12 astronauts launch to the moon on a 'pinpoint landing' lunar mission
item.description: null On Nov. 14, 1969, the Apollo 12 mission launched to the moon. This was the second moon landing of the Apollo program. The two astronauts on board were Pete Conrad , commander, and Alan Bean , the lunar module pilot. Astronaut Richard Gordon , the command module pilot, stayed in the command module and orbited the moon while his crewmates went to the surface. The astronauts made a pinpoint landing in a lunar mare called the Ocean of Storms. The previous moon mission, Apollo 11 , drifted far from the planned landing zone. But Apollo 12 landed close to a scientific target. That target was a robotic lander called Surveyor 3 . Scientists wanted to look at Surveyor 3 to see how well the spacecraft lasted on the moon since it landed there more than two years earlier. The Apollo 12 moonwalkers also performed a lot of moon science. The astronauts picked up 75 pounds of moon rocks. Most of the rocks were basalts that formed from molten lava. These basalts showed the Apollo 12 landing site is more than 3 billion years old. The Apollo 12 astronauts on NASA's second crewed moon landing mission. They are (left to right) are Charles Conrad Jr., Richard F. Gordon Jr., and Alan L. Bean. (Image credit: NASA) Why it mattered Apollo 12 proved that the Apollo 11 moon landing was not just a one-off stunt while setting the stage for even more ambitious missions. To truly explore the moon and advance our understanding of how our solar system formed, the follow-on Apollo flights needed to be able to land where the geologists had identified as areas of interest. Apollo 12, with its touchdown in proximity to the Surveyor probe, proved this was possible. The Apollo 12 astronauts visited NASA's Surveyor 3 lander and took samples of it back to Earth. (Image credit: NASA) The launch of Apollo 12 also underscored the importance of having a well-prepared Mission Control team, an asset that would be critical to outcome of the next mission, Apollo 13. The ability to recover from a complete electrical short out with the simple call of a through of a switch "SCE to AUX" proved that knowing every detail about how the spacecraft worked was key to a successful program. Want more space history? Check out our full On This Day In Space Story archive and watch our On This Day In Space videos on YouTube .

item.title: Kidnap: Police nab son over alleged N30m ransom demand from father
item.description: ​‌‍‍‍‍⁠⁠‍‍‌‍⁠The Police Command in Ebonyi has arrested two suspects for allegedly staging a kidnapping and demanding a ransom of N30 million from the father of one of them. The suspects are Fortune Onuoha and his friend, Godspower Nkwo, popularly known as Hulk. The Police Public Relations Officer (PPRO), SP Joshua Ukandu, disclosed this in a statement issued to the News Agency of Nigeria (NAN) on Saturday in Abakaliki. Ukandu said the incident was reported on Oct. 31, 2026, at about 10:30 p.m., when Onuoha’s father contacted the Command’s Control Room to report that his son had been abducted from his hostel in Ikwo Local Government Area of the state. He said the complainant also reported receiving view-once videos and voice notes showing his son tied up, alongside demands for N30 million ransom by the purported kidnappers. According to him, the abductors threatened to kill the victim if the ransom was not paid. The PPRO said that following the report, the command deployed operatives to conduct an intelligence-driven investigation to establish the circumstances surrounding the alleged abduction and identify those responsible. He said sustained surveillance and discreet investigative efforts led to a breakthrough on Nov. 5, when police operatives arrested the two suspects as they emerged from the room where they had been hiding. Ukandu quoted the Commissioner of Police in the state, Mrs Urunwa Okafor, as warning members of the public against staging kidnappings or making false claims of abduction. According to the PPRO, the commissioner said such acts inflicted severe emotional trauma on parents, guardians, and loved ones while diverting valuable police resources from addressing genuine security threats. She stressed that staging kidnappings and making false abduction claims were criminal offenses punishable under the law. The police commissioner urged members of the public to shun criminal activities and embrace lawful means of addressing their challenges. (NAN) The post Kidnap: Police nab son over alleged N30m ransom demand from father appeared first on Vanguard News .

item.title: Japan score in injury time to stun Brazil 3-2 in Singapore
item.description: Substitute Tatsuhiro Sakamoto netted his first international goal with a late winner as Japan edged Brazil 3-2 in a thrilling friendly at the National Stadium in Singapore on Saturday. A brilliant brace by Vinicius Junior had erased a two-goal deficit after strikes by Takefusa Kubo and Keito Nakamura put the Samurai Blue 2-0 up in the opening 19 minutes. But Sakamoto was in the right place to fire home after latching on to Kodai Sano’s deflected effort in stoppage time to give the Asian side a dramatic victory in front of 38,688 fans. In the first meeting between the teams since Brazil’s 2-1 win in the round of 32 at the World Cup in June, the Samurai Blue seized the early initiative with two goals in a torrid four-minute spell. On 15 minutes, a through ball by Ritsu Doan was picked up just inside the Brazilian half by Kubo who showed quick feet to cut inside Jair before firing a low effort past goalkeeper Pedro Morisco. Japan added another shortly afterwards after some fine work by Shuto Nakano, who broke down the right flank and centred for an unmarked Nakamura to calmly place a right-footed shot into the bottom corner of the net. Brazil responded with a magnificent goal by Vinicius in the 33rd minute. Zion Suzuki had made an excellent stop to deny Estevao when he bore down on goal, but the Japan goalkeeper could do little when the ball fell to Vinicius who found the top corner with a right-footed diagonal drive. Suzuki made good stops to deny Brazilian debutant Andre just before half-time and skipper Raphinha after the interval as Japan clung to their narrow lead. But the Selecao were not to be denied and Vinicius put them back on level terms in the 75th minute with another fine finish as he cut in from the left flank and launched a low right-footed effort that found the net off the right post. Brazil went close to grabbing the winner as substitute Endrick rocked the crossbar with a fierce effort and Joao Gomes sent a low shot narrowly wide. But in stoppage time, an effort by Kodai Sano took a fortunate bounce off a defender and fell nicely for Sakamoto to send the ball past Pedro Morisco. Brazil appealed for a foul in the build-up to the goal but VAR upheld the goal and Raphinha and manager Carlo Ancelotti were shown red card for their protests. Japan head coach Hajime Moriyasu is expected to step down after a friendly against Paraguay next Tuesday, but the 58-year-old is looking forward to handing over to successor Go Oiwa after a performance he described as the best of his tenure. “I’m happy that I can say that today’s match was the best match in my eight-year tenure,” he said. “While we couldn’t beat Brazil in the World Cup, we managed to show today what we could have done, and it will be a good build-up for the team for the future. “Now I need to pass the baton to the next coach, and that’s all I am focusing on.” For Ancelotti, the work will go after what he saw as an encouraging performance by his youthful side. “Apart from the result, I

item.content:encoded: Substitute Tatsuhiro Sakamoto netted his first international goal with a late winner as Japan edged Brazil 3-2 in a thrilling friendly at the National Stadium in Singapore on Saturday. A brilliant brace by Vinicius Junior had erased a two-goal deficit after strikes by Takefusa Kubo and Keito Nakamura put the Samurai Blue 2-0 up in the opening 19 minutes. But Sakamoto was in the right place to fire home after latching on to Kodai Sano’s deflected effort in stoppage time to give the Asian side a dramatic victory in front of 38,688 fans. In the first meeting between the teams since Brazil’s 2-1 win in the round of 32 at the World Cup in June, the Samurai Blue seized the early initiative with two goals in a torrid four-minute spell. On 15 minutes, a through ball by Ritsu Doan was picked up just inside the Brazilian half by Kubo who showed quick feet to cut inside Jair before firing a low effort past goalkeeper Pedro Morisco. Japan added another shortly afterwards after some fine work by Shuto Nakano, who broke down the right flank and centred for an unmarked Nakamura to calmly place a right-footed shot into the bottom corner of the net. Brazil responded with a magnificent goal by Vinicius in the 33rd minute. Zion Suzuki had made an excellent stop to deny Estevao when he bore down on goal, but the Japan goalkeeper could do little when the ball fell to Vinicius who found the top corner with a right-footed diagonal drive. Suzuki made good stops to deny Brazilian debutant Andre just before half-time and skipper Raphinha after the interval as Japan clung to their narrow lead. But the Selecao were not to be denied and Vinicius put them back on level terms in the 75th minute with another fine finish as he cut in from the left flank and launched a low right-footed effort that found the net off the right post. Brazil went close to grabbing the winner as substitute Endrick rocked the crossbar with a fierce effort and Joao Gomes sent a low shot narrowly wide. But in stoppage time, an effort by Kodai Sano took a fortunate bounce off a defender and fell nicely for Sakamoto to send the ball past Pedro Morisco. Brazil appealed for a foul in the build-up to the goal but VAR upheld the goal and Raphinha and manager Carlo Ancelotti were shown red card for their protests. Japan head coach Hajime Moriyasu is expected to step down after a friendly against Paraguay next Tuesday, but the 58-year-old is looking forward to handing over to successor Go Oiwa after a performance he described as the best of his tenure. “I’m happy that I can say that today’s match was the best match in my eight-year tenure,” he said. “While we couldn’t beat Brazil in the World Cup, we managed to show today what we could have done, and it will be a good build-up for the team for the future. “Now I need to pass the baton to the next coach, and that’s all I am focusing on.” For Ancelotti, the work will go after what he saw as an encouraging performance by his youthful side. “Apart from the result, I think for 70 minutes we played well,” said the Italian. “We played what we wanted to do, play with intensity. I am satisfied with the game we played, apart from the start, which was not good.” The post Japan score in injury time to stun Brazil 3-2 in Singapore appeared first on Vanguard News .

item.title: Mauricio Pochettino asked the US to believe in his project. Did he believe in it himself?
item.description: The coach’s tenure with the USMNT brought a whiplash of highs and lows. He met some goals but also left many with the impression he never truly bought in It did not take US men’s national team coach Mauricio Pochettino very long to take his first big swing. He’d just taken the reins of the program after a disastrous performance at the 2024 Copa América cost his predecessor his job, with the first home World Cup in three decades looming on the horizon. The federation introduced him in New York City, on the 24th floor of a building overlooking the Hudson River. In short order, he was asked about the culture surrounding the program. In his answer, he invoked the four-time World Cup champion US women. Continue reading...

item.title: The 143 best holiday gifts in 2026 – obsessively tested by the Guardian US
item.description: Shatterproof wine glasses, Jellycat plushies, ‘yoga paws’ and more gifts handpicked by our experts The best personalized gift ideas Nothing says holiday cheer quite like panic-browsing websites in pursuit of the perfect gift , toggling between 47 open tabs, eyes straining against your screen’s harsh blue light. But finding an item that elicits a squeal of delight from its recipient is one of the best parts of this time of year, when you have a little help. So we’ve curated 143 presents to reclaim holiday shopping as a joyous activity. We recruited seasoned writers and shopping experts to get into the holiday spirit early, vetting gifts across categories such as kitchen, home, tech and more. For months, we cooked, ate, traveled, hiked, ran, showered and slept with test products by our side. And we roped in our mothers, cats, dogs and the kids in our lives to make sure these gifts really work for the people (and pets!) they are meant for. Continue reading...

item.title: This tiny gamepad with dual analog thumbsticks pushes the limits of portable controllers
item.description: As much as I appreciate the ingenious design of the Nintendo Switch's Joy-Con , my family and I can't stand using them as standalone gamepads. So when we travel with the Switch 2 , we always bring at least one full-size gamepad, plus a couple of 8BitDo's Zero 2 controllers for games that don't use analog thumbsticks. I've spent years hunting for an alternative that pairs the size of the Zero 2 with as much of the functionality of a larger controller as I can get, and CRKD's new Atom Plus is nearly exactly that. But if you have larger hands like I do, you may find the gamepad's focus on portability a struggle. CRKD Atom Plus Where to Buy: $29. … Read the full story at The Verge.

item.title: Mark Your Calendars! Lagos International Theatre Festival Returns to MUSON Centre This November
item.description: The Lagos International Theatre Festival ( LITF ) returns for its 2026 edition on November 14–15 at the MUSON Centre, Lagos, bringing together an exciting programme of theatre from Nigeria and around the world. The festival, which attracts more than 25,000 attendees across its programme days, has become one of the most anticipated events on Lagos’s cultural calendar. This year’s festival is themed “The Masks We Wear”, anchored by the statement “The Stage Is Everywhere.” The theme explores the different roles and identities people assume in everyday life, while inviting audiences to consider how theatre extends beyond the traditional stage. LITF 2026 brings an international dimension to Lagos, featuring artists and productions from Kenya, Canada and Brazil alongside a diverse Nigerian programme. An international highlight is LeRa Entertainments’ Under The Mango Tree from Canada, produced by Lennette Randall , with productions from Norway, Kenya and Brazil adding further cultural and theatrical perspectives. The Nigerian programme features productions from Lagos, Abuja, Enugu and Abeokuta, including Monkey Laundry , directed by Olarotimi Fakunle ; tHERapy , directed by Tosin Adeyemi ; What You Have Become , directed by Lanre Adediwura; and Behind Closed Doors , directed by Bolanle Austen-Peters. The festival will also spotlight emerging theatre makers through productions from Atlantic Hall, Evergreen College and Children’s International School, alongside professional and independent productions. The festival experience begins ahead of the main weekend with a series of events across Lagos. On November 9, Theatre Meets Food, hosted by Hilda Baci, will bring together artists, partners, cultural leaders and members of Lagos’s creative community for an evening of food, theatre and conversation. This will be followed by Embassy Nights on November 10 and 11, celebrating international cultural exchange among diplomatic representatives, artists and creative industry leaders. The programme culminates in an Opening Night Gala on November 13, ahead of the main festival weekend at MUSON Centre on November 14 and 15. LITF 2026 is supported by the Lagos State Government, LekOil, Pillar Oil, Afrexim and Amstel , alongside its growing network of international and cultural partners. Founder of LITF, Bolanle Austen-Peters , said: “The Masks We Wear is a theme that speaks to all of us. We all play different roles in our lives, and theatre allows us to examine those roles, question them, and perhaps see ourselves differently. This year, we are also reminding audiences that theatre is not confined to a theatre building. The stage is everywhere.” Festival Director, Vanessa Jev , said the diversity of voices at this year’s festival was particularly exciting, with Nigerian artists joining performers from Kenya, Canada and Brazil to create opportunities for audiences to experience different cultures and perspectives. Founded by Bolanle Austen-Peters, LITF celebrates theatre

item.description: Loss in Singapore marred by unruly end to friendly Argentina beaten 2-1 by Uruguay in Buenos Aires Raphinha was sent off as Brazil crashed to a 3-2 defeat to Japan in their international friendly in Singapore. The Barcelona captain had been substituted after 71 minutes, but was shown a red card after protesting against Tatsuhiro Sakamoto’s stoppage-time winner on the touchline. The Brazil head coach, Carlo Ancelotti, was also sent off in a fractious ending to the match. Japan went 2-0 up inside 20 minutes through Takefusa Kubo and Keito Nakamura. Vinicius Junior reduced the deficit in the 33rd minute and scored again to drag them level on 75 minutes, before Sakamoto’s controversial late winner. Continue reading...

item.title: Her Enterprise, Africa’s Advantage: HerSphere Global Summit 2026 Convenes Africa’s Foremost Women Leaders in Lagos
item.description: Africa’s economic story is increasingly being written by women. Across the continent, women own and operate a remarkable share of small and growing enterprises, sustain household and community economies, and drive innovation in sectors from finance and technology to the creative industries. Yet the gap between participation and power remains wide. Too many women-led businesses stay small, under-capitalised and absent from the rooms where markets, policy and capital are shaped. On Tuesday, 17 November 2026, the HerSphere Global Summit 2026 will gather a distinguished assembly of leaders at the Wole Soyinka Centre, Lagos, Nigeria, to confront that gap directly. Proceedings begin promptly at 9:00 a.m. A Theme That Demands Action This year’s theme, “ Her Enterprise, Africa Advantage: Moving Women-Led Businesses Beyond Participation to Economic Power,” reflects a deliberate shift in the conversation. The question is no longer whether women belong in Africa’s economy — that has long been settled. The question is how women-led enterprises can scale, command capital, influence policy and build institutions that endure. The summit is designed to move beyond inspiration to strategy: how women founders access growth finance, how they enter regional and global value chains, how public institutions and private capital can work together to back them, and how today’s enterprises become tomorrow’s market leaders. An Exceptional Line-Up of Voices HerSphere Global Summit 2026 brings together an exceptional roster of women who have shaped Nigeria’s and Africa’s judicial, public, financial, entrepreneurial and creative landscapes: • Hon. Justice Amina Adamu Augie (CFR) • Dolapo Osinbajo • Hannatu Musa Musawa • Godrey Ogbechie • Maisie Dunbar • Bolanle Austen-Peters • Uche Pedro • Jumoke Olaniyan • Monisola Olufunke Alabi • Brenda Nwagwu • Chioma Ude • Adesuwa Okunbo Rhodes • Ifeoma Uddoh • Temilade Aduroja • Lehle Balde • Arese Ugwu Together, they represent decades of leadership across law, public service, investment, media, entertainment, financial inclusion and enterprise building — and a shared conviction that Africa’s prosperity depends on the full economic power of its women. Backed by Institutions That Shape the Economy The summit is supported by a strong coalition of partners: the Lagos State Government, the Office of Sustainable Development Goals (Lagos Global), the Nigerian Exchange Group (NGX), Delphino Entertainment, and SheMeansBusiness by BusinessDay. Their involvement underscores a growing recognition across government, capital markets and media that empowering women-led enterprise is not a social side-project — it is core economic strategy. Who Should Attend HerSphere Global Summit 2026 is for: • Women founders and business owners ready to scale • Investors, financiers and capital-market leaders seeking high-potential opportunities • Policymakers and development partners committed to inclusive growth • Corporate executives building diverse supply chai

Starship launched on its 15th test flight on Friday evening (Nov. 13), rising into the sky from SpaceX's Starbase site in South Texas. That didn't happen, however; SpaceX diverted Starship's Super Heavy booster to a controlled splashdown in the Gulf of Mexico 6.5 minutes after launch. item.content:encoded: null SpaceX plans to catch the upper stage of its Starship megarocket for the first time ever today (Nov. 14), and you can watch the action live. (SpaceX said later that a guidance and navigaton issue during its descent triggered and automatic abort . But a catch of the Ship upper stage is still on the table, and that would be historic in itself: SpaceX has never tried it before. Starship Die Cast Rocket Model Was $47.99 Now $39.99 on Amazon . Even if you can't see SpaceX's Starship in person, you can score a model of your own. Standing at 13.77 inches (35 cm), this is a 1:375 ratio of SpaceX's Starship as a desktop model. The materials here are alloy steel and it weighs just 225g. View Deal The Ship catch is scheduled to occur today at around 4:20 p.m. EST (2120 GMT; 3:20 p.m. local Texas time) — roughly 22.5 hours after Flight 15 lifted off. You can watch it live here at Space.com. There's no guarantee that it will happen, however: If SpaceX detects anything off-nominal with Ship, it will scrap the catch attempt, as it did with Super Heavy on Friday afternoon. We'll just have to wait and see. SpaceX, however, seems confident. Flight controllers decided early Saturday morning, about seven hours after liftoff, to forgo a second window to end the mission early with a splashdown off the coast of Chile. "Starship's going to stay in space. We are one step closer to an eventual return to launch site," SpaceX spokesperson Dan Huot said in a live commentary update. "So that's great news." The Ship upper stage of SpaceX's Starship megarocket circles Earth on Flight 15 on Nov. 13, 2026. (Image credit: SpaceX) While the double-catch attempt was Flight 15's main headline, the mission had other objectives as well. One was getting Ship to orbit, which had happened on just one previous Starship launch — Flight 14 , which lifted off on Sept. 28. Ship deployed 26 of SpaceX's next-gen Starlink V3 broadband satellites in low Earth orbit (LEO) on Flight 14, and it did so again on Flight 15. These 52 spacecraft are the first members of a constellation that will eventually consist of 100,000 satellites , if all goes according to SpaceX's plan. Some of those Starlink satellites took video and images of Starship's heat shield to check its health for today's landing attempt. Those images, combined with ground-based cameras, found the Ship in good shape. the company said. "Our heat shield team reviewed all the data we got from our ground tracking cameras, and from those satellite cameras and confirmed the heat shield is in a good posture for a reentry and return to the launch site," Huot said. And SpaceX plans to use Starship to build an even bigger network in LEO — Starmind, an AI data-center constellation that will harbor a million spacecraft , according to Elon Musk . (For context: SpaceX's current-gen Starlink network employs about 11,000 satellites at the moment.) Assembling these megaconstellations will require an incredible launch cadence. And the double chopstick catch is key to that vision, SpaceX says, for it will enable quicker inspection, refurbishment and reflight of Starship. So the company will doubtless try the maneuver again soon — probably on the next Starship flight, which won't be too far down the road. Editor's note: This story was updated at 8 a.m. EST to include new details on SpaceX's Starship Flight 15 mission from SpaceX. Space.com Editor-in-Chief Tariq Malik contributed to this report.

item.title: James Webb telescope finds ice older than the star it orbits
item.description: Beta Pictoris is a young star, roughly 20 million years old, and located about 64 light-years away from Earth. It is surrounded by a vast disk of dust and rubble where planets are still forming—astronomers have already found three. In a new Science study, a team led by Sarah Betti, an astronomer at the Space Telescope Science Institute in Baltimore, used the James Webb Space Telescope to look for ice in this disk. Researchers found both water and carbon dioxide ice. The water ice is glassy rather than crystalline, and it is mixed with carbon dioxide in roughly the same proportions we see in comets of our own Solar System. This suggests ingredients necessary to form water-rich worlds might be common around young stars. The missing ice Beta Pictoris is one of the best studied stars in the sky. Its disk was among the first ever imaged, back in 1984, and we see it almost exactly edge-on, which makes it a natural laboratory for studying how planetary systems grow. It's what astronomers call a debris disk, where the dust is constantly replenished by collisions among comets and planetesimals, small bodies that are the building blocks of planets. Read full article Comments

item.title: Winemakers are learning that conservation can be good for business
item.description: More than 500 vineyards are scattered across the slopes and valleys of South Africa’s Western Cape , one of the world’s most biologically diverse landscapes. The region produces about 90 percent of South Africa’s wine , but winemakers there are increasingly struggling with drought, excessive heat and erratic rainfall. Temperatures in the region have risen 1.5 to 2 times faster than the global average over the past five decades. And extreme storms have become more intense as climate variability increases. The late 2010s brought a significant challenge for winemakers, as three years of severe drought placed vineyards under intense stress and reduced grape production. As climate variability places increasing pressure on grape production, many wine producers are building on sustainability measures that have long been part of vineyard management. Read full article Comments

item.title: See Jupiter and Mars make a spectacular close approach overnight Nov. 15-16
item.description: null Heads up stargazers! Mars meets Jupiter for a spectacular rendezvous in the heart of the constellation Leo on the night of Nov. 15-16, and they won't be this close again until July 2029. Jupiter and Mars will appear a little over 1 degree from each other as they rise over the eastern horizon around midnight for viewers in the U.S., as the blue-white light of the main-sequence star Regulus glows below, according to In-The-Sky . It's all a trick of perspective, but spectacular nonetheless. In reality Mars and Jupiter are separated by a gulf of over 368 million miles (592 million kilometers), while the light from Regulus has travelled for some 79 light-years before reaching Earth . The spectacular display occurs just once every 2-2.5 years , when Mars catches up to Jupiter as it plies its more distant orbit, making the pair appear side by side from our Earthly vantage point — an event known to astronomers as an appulse. Jupiter, Mars and Regulus will appear close together on the night of Nov. 15-16. (Image credit: Created by Anthony Wood in Canva.) Both Mars and Jupiter are "superior planets" whose orbits exist beyond that of Earth. As a result their disks always appear full to us through the eyepiece of a telescope, unlike the inner planets Mercury and Venus , which exhibit moon-like phases as they circle the sun . A 6-inch telescope can reveal the wildly differing natures of the solar system worlds. Slew your scope to Jupiter to spot the gargantuan cloud bands (and zones) that ring the gas giant , formed from masses of ammonia and water that travel in different directions through Jupiter's hydrogen and helium atmosphere, driven by powerful jet streams. How to measure distances in the night sky using your outstretched hand. (Image credit: Created in Canva Pro) Mars, meanwhile, appears as a reddish, ochre disk complete with dark surface features, where basaltic rock has been scoured clean of the iron-rich dust that covers much of its surface, according to NASA . Interested in seeing and capturing the planets for yourself? Then be sure to read our guide on everything you need to observe and photograph the planets of the solar system, along with our picks of the top telescopes , cameras and lenses for exploring the night sky in 2026. Editor's Note: If you would like to share your photos of Mars and Jupiter with Space.com's readers, then please send your photo(s), comments, and your name and location to spacephotos@space.com.

item.title: Microsoft's school email bill gives rivals something to smile about
item.description: The fallout from Microsoft's education price rises and service cuts continues as institutions weigh the prospect of bigger bills, and the Windows maker's rivals struggle not to pull "I told you so" faces. The main takeaways are that free student email and collaboration services are being retired, and storage entitlements are changing. These changes generally apply at institutions' first renewal or extension on or after January 1, 2028. Microsoft announced the new plans last week, and the UK's Department for Education described itself as "disappointed" at the news. As well it might be, although the UK government has rarely seen a deal from Microsoft that it didn't like . Or, for that matter, other US tech giants . Exactly how much educational institutions will have to spend remains unclear. Mary Jo Foley of Directions on Microsoft put indicative student pricing at $2 per year for Microsoft 365 Education A2, $4 for A3, and $6 for A5, with Teams adding another dollar annually. Faculty licenses cost considerably more, while the new A7 student tier jumps to $385 a year before Teams. Foley cautioned that these were approximate figures, with actual prices set by Microsoft's partners. The new no-cost student tier, Microsoft 365 Education A0, is a poor replacement for Office 365 A1: it excludes Exchange Online, SharePoint Online, and Teams. Eligibility also requires full paid faculty coverage on A2 or higher and students who actively use Windows devices for education – potentially awkward for institutions running fleets of Chromebooks. A few dollars per student might not sound alarming. Multiply that across an institution, however, and something that used to be free becomes a recurring bill. Michael Meeks, CEO of Collabora Productivity, told The Register: "Free was the bait on the hook, and Microsoft spent years reeling in schools' email accounts, documents, identity management and classrooms onto its cloud." A poster on the edugeek.net forums commented: "This was always going to happen, I remember thinking this when we moved over to the MS free cloud solution. It will be free until they decide it isn't." The risk for Microsoft is that there are options. Meeks told us: "Schools now have a year to plan, and, in our experience with other large-scale educational projects, such as the University of Lille, that can be enough time to migrate properly." Other options include Nextcloud, which will be rolled out as part of Germany's Educational Cloud Infrastructure . Several Swiss universities also migrated to the service over an August weekend. According to Nextcloud, 39,500 students, teachers, and researchers, along with 585 terabytes of data, were shifted. Both Nextcloud and Collabora Productivity also highlight another factor that could drive educational institutions away from Microsoft: sovereignty. item.content:encoded: The fallout from Microsoft's education price rises and service cuts continues as institutions weigh the prospect of bigger bills, and the Windows maker's rivals struggle not to pull "I told you so" faces. The main takeaways are that free student email and collaboration services are being retired, and storage entitlements are changing. These changes generally apply at institutions' first renewal or extension on or after January 1, 2028. Microsoft announced the new plans last week, and the UK's Department for Education described itself as "disappointed" at the news. As well it might be, although the UK government has rarely seen a deal from Microsoft that it didn't like . Or, for that matter, other US tech giants . Exactly how much educational institutions will have to spend remains unclear. Mary Jo Foley of Directions on Microsoft put indicative student pricing at $2 per year for Microsoft 365 Education A2, $4 for A3, and $6 for A5, with Teams adding another dollar annually. Faculty licenses cost considerably more, while the new A7 student tier jumps to $385 a year before Teams. Foley cautioned that these were approximate figures, with actual prices set by Microsoft's partners. The new no-cost student tier, Microsoft 365 Education A0, is a poor replacement for Office 365 A1: it excludes Exchange Online, SharePoint Online, and Teams. Eligibility also requires full paid faculty coverage on A2 or higher and students who actively use Windows devices for education – potentially awkward for institutions running fleets of Chromebooks. A few dollars per student might not sound alarming. Multiply that across an institution, however, and something that used to be free becomes a recurring bill. Michael Meeks, CEO of Collabora Productivity, told The Register: "Free was the bait on the hook, and Microsoft spent years reeling in schools' email accounts, documents, identity management and classrooms onto its cloud." A poster on the edugeek.net forums commented: "This was always going to happen, I remember thinking this when we moved over to the MS free cloud solution. It will be free until they decide it isn't." The risk for Microsoft is that there are options. Meeks told us: "Schools now have a year to plan, and, in our experience with other large-scale educational projects, such as the University of Lille, that can be enough time to migrate properly." Other options include Nextcloud, which will be rolled out as part of Germany's Educational Cloud Infrastructure . Several Swiss universities also migrated to the service over an August weekend. According to Nextcloud, 39,500 students, teachers, and researchers, along with 585 terabytes of data, were shifted. Both Nextcloud and Collabora Productivity also highlight another factor that could drive educational institutions away from Microsoft: sovereignty. Dr Patrick Alberts, managing director of messaging provider Element, told The Register : "When an organization is locked to a vendor, it should be no surprise when that vendor takes advantage. When switching is made difficult, the vendor holds all the leverage. They can raise prices or slash services on a whim, knowing customers will swallow the pain rather than rip out the infrastructure. "Yet it's a bold move, given European governments are proactively following a digitally sovereign strategy." Switching suppliers still takes planning, and the alternatives won't necessarily replace every Microsoft service. But the Windows behemoth has given educational institutions a fresh reason to investigate – and its rivals a particularly convenient opening pitch. ®

item.title: Can Nvidia survive without tech titan Jensen Huang?
item.description: The Financial Times says computing giant Nvidia has approached Rene Haas, CEO of British chip designer Arm, in its search for a potential successor to Jensen Huang. Huang resigned after his affair with an alleged Chinese spy. Meanwhile some employees are clamouring for Huang's return – as his fellow tech leader Elon Musk. A sign of Huang's lingering star power, in an industry where so often the fate of each giant company depends on one man. Story by Peter O'Brien.

Campaign groups, students and Yellow Vest protesters are due to join forces in the capital, bringing together demands on wages, education and civil liberties. item.title: US nationwide flight ground stop: "Our routers got overloaded with data"
item.description: On Friday, the Federal Aviation Administration issued a rare nationwide ground stop. More than 8,200 flights, or over 31% of those scheduled in the United States, were canceled. The ground stop lasted nearly five hours and was the longest in the country since September 11, 2001. Officials blamed outdated air traffic communications equipment, and said that there was no evidence of a cyber attack. The airspace is now reopened and flights have resumed.

item.title: Big Tech takes a beating as online safety experts accuse companies of doing bare minimum
item.description: Technology companies are doing just enough to show a degree of compliance with the UK's Online Safety Act, but are failing to meet the needs of the individuals and young victims the legislation exists to protect, experts say. A panel of online safety pros assembled before Parliament's Communications and Digital Committee on Tuesday, taking aim at the likes of Google, Microsoft, Meta, and ByteDance for failing to act on important matters. Clare McGlynn, professor of law at Durham University and expert on violence against women and girls (VAWG), was especially critical of major search engine providers for their inconsistent downranking of harmful content search terms. "Rape porn," for example, is correctly downranked and no user sees any relevant links until the tenth page of results, although adjacent terms such as "unwilling porn" can be found as early as the third page, McGlynn said. "I just think if someone spent a little more time thinking 'I really want to minimize the risk of this material appearing,' I would take a systematic approach," she told the committee. "I would downrank 'unwilling' and 'unwanted,' and I would downrank 'asleep porn' as well… because it just means that it's easily findable. "So, they don't rank some of them, but just not systematically or wholly consistently." McGlynn went on to say that during her own research, "force porn" was rightly downranked heavily, although terms as similar as "forced porn" were not. "If you were trying to think of the words that would be similar to say rape, and rape porn is extreme porn and it's not supposed to be on those platforms anymore, you would think of words like unwilling and unwanted," she added. "And we know your algorithm would." Google inevitably took much of McGlynn's flak due to its dominance of the search engine market, although the professor said the same issues can be observed on Bing, too. Alexandra Whiston-Dew, partner at law firm Miscon de Raya, argued that search engines have such an important role in regulating the OSA, noting the limited resources at Ofcom's disposal. She said that more needs to be done from the tech side to ensure different parties in the chain of publication are detected early and downranked or blocked accordingly. There are publications, for example, that actively advertise themselves as websites that host illegal content, and these appear to be missing from the search engines' crosshairs. "So, they are spotlighting the fact that they are publishing illegal content, and this is going under the radar not only from the search engines but also the other platforms and the businesses in the chain of publication," said Whiston-Dew. "Also Ofcom needs to really pull all of their resources together and attack that receptacle of illegal content." Similarly, McGlynn raised the issue of porn sites continuing to host extreme porn, as they are legally allowed to do, to make it available to less regulated territories. item.content:encoded: Technology companies are doing just enough to show a degree of compliance with the UK's Online Safety Act, but are failing to meet the needs of the individuals and young victims the legislation exists to protect, experts say. A panel of online safety pros assembled before Parliament's Communications and Digital Committee on Tuesday, taking aim at the likes of Google, Microsoft, Meta, and ByteDance for failing to act on important matters. Clare McGlynn, professor of law at Durham University and expert on violence against women and girls (VAWG), was especially critical of major search engine providers for their inconsistent downranking of harmful content search terms. "Rape porn," for example, is correctly downranked and no user sees any relevant links until the tenth page of results, although adjacent terms such as "unwilling porn" can be found as early as the third page, McGlynn said. "I just think if someone spent a little more time thinking 'I really want to minimize the risk of this material appearing,' I would take a systematic approach," she told the committee. "I would downrank 'unwilling' and 'unwanted,' and I would downrank 'asleep porn' as well… because it just means that it's easily findable. "So, they don't rank some of them, but just not systematically or wholly consistently." McGlynn went on to say that during her own research, "force porn" was rightly downranked heavily, although terms as similar as "forced porn" were not. "If you were trying to think of the words that would be similar to say rape, and rape porn is extreme porn and it's not supposed to be on those platforms anymore, you would think of words like unwilling and unwanted," she added. "And we know your algorithm would." Google inevitably took much of McGlynn's flak due to its dominance of the search engine market, although the professor said the same issues can be observed on Bing, too. Alexandra Whiston-Dew, partner at law firm Miscon de Raya, argued that search engines have such an important role in regulating the OSA, noting the limited resources at Ofcom's disposal. She said that more needs to be done from the tech side to ensure different parties in the chain of publication are detected early and downranked or blocked accordingly. There are publications, for example, that actively advertise themselves as websites that host illegal content, and these appear to be missing from the search engines' crosshairs. "So, they are spotlighting the fact that they are publishing illegal content, and this is going under the radar not only from the search engines but also the other platforms and the businesses in the chain of publication," said Whiston-Dew. "Also Ofcom needs to really pull all of their resources together and attack that receptacle of illegal content." Similarly, McGlynn raised the issue of porn sites continuing to host extreme porn, as they are legally allowed to do, to make it available to less regulated territories. With the harmful content still on the site, all it takes is a VPN connection to access it, and bypass the age assurance mechanisms in the process. Success of user reports trails away As well as a piecemeal approach to downranking extreme content, experts said that tech platforms initially showed a strong appetite in quickly handling content-takedown requests, although this appears to have waned substantially. Citing data from domestic violence and VAWG charity Refuge [PDF], Janaya Walker, interim director at the End Violence Against Women Coalition (EVAW), said that before November 2025, the success rate for these kinds of reports made using Refuge’s Trusted Flagger team stood at 53.7 percent. Over the past 12 months, however, this dropped to just 18.2 percent. Further, since November 2025, zero percent of reports made to Meta have been successful, according to Refuge’s figures. The charity’s Trusted Flagger team works closely with social media platforms to report content that victims may have reported to it. The idea is that if the report comes from an authority like Refuge, it is acted upon more quickly. Walker said there was real concern about how platforms behave and whether they comply with existing regulation, and about what that means for specialist services supporting survivors in limo, particularly without an online commission to advocate for victims' and survivors' interests. Meta did not immediately respond to questions about its takedown rate, but according to its Community Standards Enforcement Report , it removed 27.8 million posts related to adult nudity and sexual activity between April and June 2026. The report does not include a category devoted to VAWG-related reports, so take the data with the appropriate level of scrutiny. Neither Google, Microsoft, nor TikTok responded to requests for comment. The findings from Refuge and the discussion in Parliament this week reflect the wider concern about the efficacy of the OSA, and how online safety experts are frustrated with how little impact it has had, more than a year after the new duties came into force. England's Children's Commissioner, Dame Rachel de Souza, told the same committee in September that the OSA "has made absolutely no difference " to children's access to harmful content online, as evidenced by the accounts of young people themselves. Amid discussions from the panel of experts this week regarding the need for a civil redress scheme, McGlynn pointed to British Columbia's system as an example of how other countries are going further to protect people from online harms. She said: "...an individual still does not have the right to demand an image be taken down. And that is where I think we just lack that capacity to say to an individual, 'this is what you need to do, and you can bring this legal action, for example, against X, against the perpetrator, you can get the material deleted.' "In British Columbia in Canada, they have a swift online civil redress system where you can make these claims, and you can get instant orders to get this material taken down, and you can even get compensation for some of the harm suffered. "So other countries are doing more, if you like, to give the individuals that right as well as all the other measures at the platform level." ®

item.title: De la Fuente feels the strain as Lamine Yamal club v country debate rages in Spain
item.description: Head coach hits out at ‘lies’ as suggestions of preferential treatment for young star overshadow preparations for England game in Madrid From the London Palladium to Madrid’s Metropolitano, they’re all here. On Sunday night, the footballers who lifted the game’s biggest awards meet again three weeks later and on the field this time, dinner jackets but not a single man left behind. Harry Kane, the Ballon d’Or and Gerd Müller trophy winner. Unai Simón, holder of the Lev Yashin award . Luis de la Fuente , the coach of the year who on Thursday night announced that also joining them will be Lamine Yamal , the kid who lifted the Kopa award as the best young player for the third year running and said he would have preferred Pau Cubarsí to be standing there instead. And, yes, Cubarsí will be there too for the final Nations League group game. At 1.45pm on Friday the world and European champions landed back at Madrid’s Barajas airport from Prague, where they had won again, before making their way by bus to their Las Rozas HQ, around the M40 motorway to the north-west of the capital. At about the same time, Lamine Yamal arrived from Barcelona, due in at midday. As was Mikel Oyarzabal , scorer of the winner at Euro 2024 and Spain’s top marksman this summer (not that he would ever tell you so) from San Sebastián. At 7.30pm, they trained, preparing to meet the World Cup semi-finalists and the team they defeated in Berlin at the end of Euro 2024. Two starters from the World Cup final will be absent: Dani Olmo and the captain, 2024 Ballon d’Or winner Rodri , are injured. But everyone else will be there. Continue reading...

item.title: New Scientist readers on how the magazine has shaped their lives
item.description: Have you been reading New Scientist since the start? Getty Images/Westend61 The first issue of New Scientist was published on 22 November 1956, and some of our readers have been with us since the very beginning. We asked subscribers, young and old, to tell us how they first encountered the magazine and how New Scientist has influenced their lives. The volume of responses and the gratitude expressed within them were quite overwhelming. Here are some of our favourites, featuring a spectacular maggot experiment, science-inspired poetry and even a match made on the short-lived New Scientist dating site. Huge thanks to everyone who wrote in. I was interested to see that New Scientist was launched “for all those men and women who are interested in scientific discovery and in its industrial, commercial and social consequences”. At the age of 13, I saved up a shilling from my Saturday morning “jobs” to purchase the first edition on 22 November 1956 and became one of those people interested in scientific discovery. Seventy years later, I remain a subscriber, after a scientific career that took me to many (if not, most!) countries in the world. New Scientist covered things like the opening of Jodrell Bank telescope in 1957. Since that was only about 50 miles (80 kilometres) away, it necessitated a bike ride to see what it really looked like! Peter Hall Advertisement I seem to have been reading New Scientist for the full 70! I do recall my encounter with the first edition: I was at Bec Grammar School in south London in a second-year physics class – it was 1956. The teacher, a genial boffin-type, announced the advent of the new publication and handed out copies – all I remember is its grey (or was it beige?) pages, which I read in a perfunctory way (I was only 12!) little thinking it would follow me through life and around the globe. Robyn Williams I was at Malvern College in England for my O level examinations from 1955 to 1958. My science master at Malvern had recognised my interest in science and technology and he bought the very first issue of New Scientist with his own money. At the next science class, he stood up in front of the whole class and waved the first issue, saying, “Young Inman, a new UK science and technology magazine has been published and here is the first issue for you.” I went on to reach 60 years as a member of the UK Institution of Civil Engineers. Peter Inman 1956 puts me back at school – Fettes College in Edinburgh. The school adopted New Scientist from its first edition and it was available in the library, where senior boys interested in science were recommended to read it. And so began a lifetime of New Scientist – I have been a regular for as long as I can remember and a subscriber for a very long time. I am very grateful to New Scientist for maintaining my interest in all the sciences and new developments, which I am sure has helped me to think laterally and to have a greater understanding of what makes everything tick. Frank Eva
item.dc:creator: Sam Wong
item.content:encoded: Have you been reading New Scientist since the start? Getty Images/Westend61 The first issue of New Scientist was published on 22 November 1956, and some of our readers have been with us since the very beginning. At the age of 13, I saved up a shilling from my Saturday morning “jobs” to purchase the first edition on 22 November 1956 and became one of those people interested in scientific discovery. Peter Hall Advertisement I seem to have been reading New Scientist for the full 70! I do recall my encounter with the first edition: I was at Bec Grammar School in south London in a second-year physics class – it was 1956. The teacher, a genial boffin-type, announced the advent of the new publication and handed out copies – all I remember is its grey (or was it beige?) pages, which I read in a perfunctory way (I was only 12!) little thinking it would follow me through life and around the globe. Robyn Williams I was at Malvern College in England for my O level examinations from 1955 to 1958. My science master at Malvern had recognised my interest in science and technology and he bought the very first issue of New Scientist with his own money. At the next science class, he stood up in front of the whole class and waved the first issue, saying, “Young Inman, a new UK science and technology magazine has been published and here is the first issue for you.” I went on to reach 60 years as a member of the UK Institution of Civil Engineers. Peter Inman 1956 puts me back at school – Fettes College in Edinburgh. The school adopted New Scientist from its first edition and it was available in the library, where senior boys interested in science were recommended to read it. And so began a lifetime of New Scientist – I have been a regular for as long as I can remember and a subscriber for a very long time. I am very grateful to New Scientist for maintaining my interest in all the sciences and new developments, which I am sure has helped me to think laterally and to have a greater understanding of what makes everything tick. Frank Evans As a pupil in the mid-1960s at a girls’ grammar school in the north of England, one day I picked up a copy of New Scientist in the library. I was mind-blown by an article about Albert Einstein’s theories of relativity and time dilation, including a coloured diagram! I went on to study physical and material sciences at university and worked for eight years in research. But motherhood and misogyny (in those days before equal opportunities legislation) led me to change tack and I’ve been making pottery by hand for over 55 years. I like to think my science education hasn’t been wasted, but handed down to my daughters, one of whom reads New Scientist online in France. Every week, the paper issue landing on my doormat is devoured with excitement! Anne Rodgers Read more Trustworthy science journalism is more essential than ever The stories that most interested me were about emerging electronics, the Sputnik satellite and the launch of Laika the space dog. The last of these prompted me to construct a module to house a maggot atop a 3-pence standard firework rocket and launch it. I later recovered the maggot unharmed and used it as fishing bait the next day. Mel We are a group of 12 ladies “of a certain age” who meet once a month to discuss three or four articles from New Scientist . We tackle topics such as AI, quantum computing and cosmology – all of which are quite daunting! We persevere and continue to try to understand topics like these that are very challenging. We look up terms and concepts we don’t understand and then teach each other. We also love to read articles on climate change and medical science, as these feel more relatable. We plan to get the recordings of the talks from October’s New Scientist Live , so we can watch together and discuss. We want to thank you for making science accessible to us – we all feel that it’s important as we get older to not give in to the temptation to ignore all the new discoveries and changes in the world. Diana Currie, Dawn Segrue and the Marlow Science Group An article about Benjamin Libet’s experiments in the 1980s showing there was a time gap between the brain making a decision and conscious awareness of that decision inspired me, as a psychotherapist, to find a way of using that gap in the field of psychological therapy. Two years of exploration and testing later, I taught the first cohort of students, and now it is being employed by psychologists, counsellors, psychiatrists and psychotherapists all over the world. Terence Watts 4 of the most memorable biotech moments in modern scientific history On the eve of New Scientist’s 70th anniversary, newsroom legend Andy Coghlan reveals four of the most dramatic and surprising moments from his storied career Back in 2019, I stumbled across an eye-catching magazine on the shelves of a Tesco store. The title-page article caught my eye: “Does this one microbe cause all these conditions… and does that mean we can beat them?” It was at that moment that I truly fell in love with biology. Years have passed, and I have since graduated with a science degree from the University of Edinburgh and am now a returning student at my alma mater pursuing a master of research postgraduate degree in life sciences. One day, I aim to be able to contribute – even if just a little – to aiding humanity in its endless fight against malady and illness. All of my academic achievements thus far may very well not have been possible had it not been for that magazine that caught my eye, that day in August 2019. And for that, I quite literally owe New Scientist all my academic achievements, and all that I have done, to this day. Stephen Wang I am 87 and have been reading New Scientist every week since October 1964. I still have a note from my grandson, Maximilian, from when he was 5 years old, thanking me for reading New Scientist with him. He is now studying biology at my one-time college, Merton, at the University of Oxford. In the meantime, he has already succeeded, while travelling with his mother in Amazonia, in identifying, describing, naming and publishing a new genus and species of damselfly. He and I continue to discuss issues like evolution together, though I am a classicist by training. Anthony J. Nieduszynski Your magazine is vital to our family. It sparks many conversations at the kitchen table. Our 11-year-old grandson keeps beating us to the latest issue. Our 6-year-old grandson has been enthralled with the cover art since he was 3. I cut out the cartoons and post them on the fridge. They have become the “cartoon of the week”. Often my grandsons see details I didn’t even catch. Krystyna Rodriguez The 12 strangest science stories we can’t stop thinking about From subconscious finger sniffing to rats driving cars, New Scientist staff have reported on many weird, wild or utterly bonkers discoveries and inventions in the 70 years since we began I have been a reader for almost all the publication’s life, as I first starte

item.title: Portugal did the extraordinary with Cristiano Ronaldo. Can they do it without him?
item.description: The captain, the talisman, the brand: former teammates and experts discuss Portugal entering a new era after 23 years There are days football fans hope will never come. For Portugal, this is one of them. For 23 years, Cristiano Ronaldo has been more than the country’s greatest footballer; he has been its defining sporting figure, a symbol of national pride and constant presence in the lives of supporters. After 234 appearances and 146 goals, the No 7 brought that chapter to a close and on Saturday night the team will play their first game without him . The national side are losing more than a great footballer; they are also losing one of the world’s biggest brands. Daniel Sá, the executive director of the Portuguese institute of marketing administration, believes Portugal require reinvention to attract at least some of the millions of viewers who tuned in because of CR7. Continue reading...

item.title: Starship flight 15 powers to orbit—setting up a possible catch on Saturday
item.description: STARBASE, Texas—Starship lifted off right on schedule Friday from South Texas, making its 15th test flight in more than three years. The largely successful launch took place in the early evening; as the massive rocket rose into the atmosphere, the Sun sank toward the western horizon. Conditions were ideal for the launch, with the atmospheric winds so calm the rocket’s white plume did not dissipate for many minutes. The weather in South Texas is not always comfortable; summers are long and hot. Friday evening was perfect at Starbase. The first stage ascended toward space flawlessly, releasing the upper stage above the Gulf of Mexico. From there, the Starship upper stage ignited its Raptor engines and powered its way into a nominal orbit. This was the second time SpaceX has flown Starship into low-Earth orbit. Read full article Comments

item.title: Amazon has a plan to index the world’s online shopping data
item.description: Amazon has plans to build a vault of data on every product sold anywhere on the internet, even products Amazon doesn't sell, and make the information available through its own site, according to Reuters . The project, called the "World Product Graph," is meant to make it less likely that shoppers leave Amazon to do their product research on Reddit or Google, and make it more likely shoppers end up at Amazon even if they're searching for a product sold elsewhere. The same goes for AI agents - if Amazon has the largest stockpile of shopping data, AI agents may rely on its index of products over others, so even people shopping with bots will end … Read the full story at The Verge.

item.title: SpaceX launches Starship on ambitious 22-hour Flight 15 test, but aborts booster 'chopsticks' catch (video)
item.description: null STARBASE, Texas — SpaceX launched the 15th test flight of its massive Starship rocket today (Nov. 13) and is preparing the vehicle's upper stage for its first-ever return to the launch site in less than 24 hours. Flight 15 lifted off from SpaceX 's Starbase facility here in South Texas at 5:47 p.m. ET (2247 GMT; 4:47 p.m. local Texas time). The towering Super Heavy booster and Ship upper stage cleared the tower without incident and climbed into the skies under more than 18 million pounds of thrust from the booster's 33 Raptor 3 engines. The flight continued nominally through its initial ascent, with the successful execution of Super Heavy's main engine cutoff and Ship's subsequent hot-staging — firing its own Raptors during separation from the booster — about 2.5 minutes after launch. Following stage separation, Super Heavy reoriented for a planned return to Starbase as Ship powered its way toward low Earth orbit (LEO). SpaceX originally planned to catch Super Heavy with the Starbase launch tower's giant mechanical "chopstick" arms. But it wasn't to be: The company called off the catch attempt and brought the booster down for a controlled splashdown in the Gulf of Mexico about 6.5 minutes after launch, for reasons that were not immediately clear. A successful catch would have been a significant milestone for SpaceX and its efforts to design Starship as a fully and rapidly reusable launch vehicle. It would have been the first successful recovery of a Version 3 (V3) Super Heavy , which SpaceX began flying earlier this year. The company previously recovered three of its V1 Super Heavy vehicles and reused two of those in later flights. SpaceX's Starship megarocket launches on its 15th test flight from Starbase, Texas on Nov. 13, 2026. "We’ve got a nominal orbit insertion, so Starship now in orbit around Earth for the second time ever," SpaceX's Dan Huot said during today's Flight 15 launch webcast. "That’s a really great moment."
