item.title: The 'eclipse of the century' will plunge these 8 wonders of the Roman Empire into darkness on Aug. 2, 2027
item.description: null Ancient Egyptian temples will inevitably dominate the story of the total solar eclipse on Aug. 2, 2027 . After all, the path of totality crosses Luxor, home to Karnak, the Valley of the Kings, and some of the ancient world's most famous monuments. But follow the moon 's shadow west and another ancient civilization comes into view. Before reaching Egypt, totality will sweep across the Mediterranean and North Africa, passing over an extraordinary collection of Roman cities, fortresses, theaters, temples and triumphal arches. Many lie within what became Rome's North African provinces, a region that produced some of the empire's wealthiest and most impressive cities. From beachside Baelo Claudia in Spain and military Tamuda in Morocco to Timgad and Djémila in Algeria and the jaw-dropping El Jem Amphitheater in Tunisia, Roman ruins will experience between two and more than five minutes of darkness — creating extraordinary possibilities for eclipse chasers and photographers. Here are some of the best places to watch the moon's shadow cross what was once the Roman Empire. All times, totality durations and historical cloud cover data come from Time and Date . 1. Baelo Claudia, Spain Baelo Claudia's Roman ruins overlook Bolonia beach and the Strait of Gibraltar. (Image credit: Andrea Pucci via Getty Images) Location: near Tarifa, Andalucía, Spain Start of totality and duration: 10:44 a.m. CEST; 4 minutes, 31 seconds Historical cloud cover: 12% Altitude of the sun: 37 degrees above east Roman ruins, an Atlantic beach and the mountains of Africa could all share the frame with the eclipsed sun at Baelo Claudia. Founded in the second century B.C., this remarkably well-preserved Roman city near Bolonia beach includes a forum, basilica, theater, temples, baths and a decumanus maximus (east-west street), all set against forested hills and a vast coastal sand dune. For photographers, the possibilities are exceptional — columns and temples may provide an ancient foreground, while wider compositions could incorporate the beach and dunes. On particularly clear days, Morocco is visible across the Strait of Gibraltar — potentially putting Roman ruins, two continents and a total solar eclipse into one extraordinary scene. 2. Málaga Roman Theatre, Spain The Roman Theatre at the foot of the Málaga Alcazaba dates back to the 1st century BC. item.content:encoded: null Ancient Egyptian temples will inevitably dominate the story of the total solar eclipse on Aug. 2, 2027 . After all, the path of totality crosses Luxor, home to Karnak, the Valley of the Kings, and some of the ancient world's most famous monuments. But follow the moon 's shadow west and another ancient civilization comes into view. Before reaching Egypt, totality will sweep across the Mediterranean and North Africa, passing over an extraordinary collection of Roman cities, fortresses, theaters, temples and triumphal arches. Many lie within what became Rome's North African provinces, a region that produced some of the empire's wealthiest and most impressive cities. From beachside Baelo Claudia in Spain and military Tamuda in Morocco to Timgad and Djémila in Algeria and the jaw-dropping El Jem Amphitheater in Tunisia, Roman ruins will experience between two and more than five minutes of darkness — creating extraordinary possibilities for eclipse chasers and photographers. Here are some of the best places to watch the moon's shadow cross what was once the Roman Empire. All times, totality durations and historical cloud cover data come from Time and Date . 1. Baelo Claudia, Spain Baelo Claudia's Roman ruins overlook Bolonia beach and the Strait of Gibraltar. (Image credit: Andrea Pucci via Getty Images) Location: near Tarifa, Andalucía, Spain Start of totality and duration: 10:44 a.m. CEST; 4 minutes, 31 seconds Historical cloud cover: 12% Altitude of the sun: 37 degrees above east Roman ruins, an Atlantic beach and the mountains of Africa could all share the frame with the eclipsed sun at Baelo Claudia. Founded in the second century B.C., this remarkably well-preserved Roman city near Bolonia beach includes a forum, basilica, theater, temples, baths and a decumanus maximus (east-west street), all set against forested hills and a vast coastal sand dune. For photographers, the possibilities are exceptional — columns and temples may provide an ancient foreground, while wider compositions could incorporate the beach and dunes. On particularly clear days, Morocco is visible across the Strait of Gibraltar — potentially putting Roman ruins, two continents and a total solar eclipse into one extraordinary scene. 2. Málaga Roman Theatre, Spain The Roman Theatre at the foot of the Málaga Alcazaba dates back to the 1st century BC. (Image credit: Manfred Gottschalk via Getty Images) Location: Málaga, Spain Start of totality and duration: 10:48 a.m. CEST; 1 minute, 57 seconds Historical cloud cover: 9% Altitude of the sun: 39 degrees above east Few eclipse locations can offer two civilizations in the same photograph. Málaga's Roman Theatre was built in the first century B.C., when the city was part of the Roman province of Hispania, and today sits directly beneath the Alcazaba, the imposing Muslim-era palace-fortress that dominates the hillside above. Although its totality is considerably shorter than locations farther south, the photographic possibilities are compelling. From a carefully chosen position, it may be possible to frame the darkened sun with the theater's ancient stonework and the walls of the Alcazaba rising behind it. Another major advantage for eclipse chasers is that this extraordinary historical setting sits in the heart of Málaga, making it one of the most accessible ancient sites on the path of totality. 3. Tamuda, Morocco The ruins of Tamuda near Tétouan preserve a Roman military fortress. (Image credit: Carole Raddato via Wikipedia CC BY-SA 2.0 ) Location: Tétouan, Morocco Start of totality and duration: 08:45 a.m. GMT; 4 minutes, 51 seconds Historical cloud cover: 14% Altitude of sun: 38 degrees above east-southeast Long before the Romans arrived in northern Morocco, Tamuda was already a thriving Mauretanian settlement. Founded around the third century B.C. in the Martil Valley, near modern Tétouan, the Romans established a fortified military camp here in the first century A.D., whose massive stone walls remain the defining feature of this archaeological site. Tamuda combines long totality, promising weather and an atmospheric archaeological foreground — yet remains far less famous than the Roman sites across the Strait of Gibraltar. 4. Timgad, Algeria The Roman Arch of Timgad, Algeria. (Image credit: Antonio Ciufo via Getty Images) Location: near Batna, Algeria Start of totality and duration: 10:01 a.m. CET; 5 minutes, 20 seconds Historical cloud cover: 5% Altitude of sun: 51 degrees above east-southeast Few places in the 2027 path of totality combine ancient architecture and long totality quite like Timgad. Founded around A.D. 100 as the Roman colony of Thamugadi, this remarkably well-preserved city sits on an open plateau at the foot of Algeria's Aurès Mountains. Its grid of streets, forum, theater, temples, baths and columns survives alongside its most famous monument, the three-arched gateway traditionally known as the Arch of Trajan. A relatively high sun will make close architectural compositions challenging, but Timgad's wide-open site provides plenty of possibilities for carefully planned wide-angle images. 5. Lambaesis, Algeria Arch of Commodus at the Roman site of Lambaesis, Algeria. (Image credit: Ethel Davies / robertharding via Getty Images) Location: near Batna, Algeria Start of totality and duration: 10:01 a.m. CET; 5 minutes, 20 seconds Historical cloud cover: 5% Altitude of sun: 51 degrees above east-southeast Just 12—15 miles (20—25 km) west of Timgad lies its military counterpart. Lambaesis was the principal base of Rome's Legio III Augusta, the legion that helped secure Rome's African Empire. Rather than an entire gridded colonial city, the attraction here is monumental military architecture, most notably the imposing remains of the heart of the fortress. The eclipse circumstances are almost identical to nearby Timgad, with more than five minutes of totality and historically excellent prospects for clear skies. Scout both sites beforehand, study where the sun will stand above the ruins, and decide which offers the strongest alignment — and the easiest access — on eclipse morning. 6. Djémila, Algeria The mountain setting of Djémila, ancient Cuicul, could provide a dramatic backdrop to just over two minutes of totality. (Image credit: Nirian via Getty Images) Location: Djémila, Algeria Start of totality and duration: 10:02 a.m. CET; 2 minutes, 2 seconds Historical cloud cover: 11% Altitude of eclipsed sun: 50 degrees above east-southeast Djémila trades a long eclipse for one of the most spectacular settings on the path of totality. Known to the Romans as Cuicul, this exceptionally well-preserved city was built in mountainous terrain around 2,950 feet (900 meters) above sea level — an unusual setting for a Roman settlement — and its ruins include temples, forums, houses, baths, arches and a theater. The surrounding green hills and mountains give eclipse photographers a very different backdrop from the flatter, more arid landscapes farther south. The catch is totality, which is significantly shorter than at other Roman ruins. 7. Sbeitla, Tunisia The Roman temples of ancient Sufetula at Sbeitla, Tunisia. (Image credit: Renee Vititoe via Getty Images) Location: Kasserine, Tunisia Start of totality and duration: 10:06 a.m. CET; 5 minutes, 19 seconds Historical cloud cover: 4% Altitude of sun: 54 degrees above east-southeast Sbeitla could be one of the great archaeological settings for the 2027 eclipse. Known in Roman times as Sufetula, the city prospered under Roman rule and today contains some of Tunisia's most impressive ancient ruins. Its centerpiece is an unusual group of three remarkably well-preserved temples dedicated to Jupiter, Juno and Minerva, standing above the forum and reached through the monumental Arch of Antoninus Pius. item.title: Quantum leap: IBM plans to scale beyond 1,000 qubits in 2027 with Nighthawk r3 processor
item.description: IBM has unveiled the Nighthawk r3, an upcoming next-gen quantum processor that will feature 520 qubits, as another step towards a planned fault-tolerant quantum system it hopes to launch in 2029. Big Blue's current Nighthawk r2 was only made available in September and features 120 quantum bits (qubits) capable of handling circuits using 7,500 operations. Its successor, IBM claims, will have more than four times as many qubits and execute 10,000 quantum operations to tackle larger, more complex problems while maintaining the same speed and accuracy. Nighthawk r3 is slated to arrive in 2027, when Big Blue plans to link two of the quantum processors into a single system with more than 1,000 qubits. IBM said applications increasingly require circuits executing thousands of quantum operations on approximately 100 qubits or more, speeding up collection of the millions or billions of samples needed to perform complex computations. Speed determines whether such demanding workloads can be completed in practical timeframes and at a reasonable cost. The new quantum processor will feature 10 chip-to-chip interconnects, called l-couplers, designed for linking together processors that it will use to enable a single 1,040-qubit system. This tech was tested using Nighthawk r1 processors . IBM previously outlined its goal of reaching reliable error correcting territory in 2029 with a quantum processor codenamed Starling. Now it intends for this to be the world’s first fault-tolerant quantum computer , capable of running quantum circuits comprising 100 million quantum operations on 200 logical qubits. This is an ambitious goal, considering fault-tolerant quantum technology always seems to be at least a decade away, despite numerous breakthroughs and technology introductions. However, some in the technology industry believe the odds on a working system are shortening , given the increased activity around making encryption ready with support for quantum-resistant algorithms. Then again, a professor at the University of Auckland New Zealand famously claimed last year that quantum computers hadn't so far managed to factor any number greater than 21 without cheating. IBM presented a framework for Starling in a 2025 paper outlining hardware to implement the improbably named bivariate bicycle quantum low-density parity check (qLDPC) error correction codes. These significantly reduce the number of physical qubits needed to store and process quantum information, compared to existing surface codes. Using the architecture in the paper, Big Blue intends to assemble Starling from modules that each contain a quantum memory and logical processing unit (LPU), allowing logic operations on the memory. The modules will have universal adapters letting them connect using l-couplers. IBM is also preparing the way ahead by combining its quantum processors with classical high-performance compute (HPC) systems to research better quantum error correction. Then again, a professor at the University of Auckland New Zealand famously claimed last year that quantum computers hadn't so far managed to factor any number greater than 21 without cheating. IBM presented a framework for Starling in a 2025 paper outlining hardware to implement the improbably named bivariate bicycle quantum low-density parity check (qLDPC) error correction codes. Last week, Oak Ridge National Laboratory (ORNL) in the US announced such a system , combining an IBM Quantum System Two with Nighthawk r2 quantum processors and Umbra, powered by AMD 5th Gen Epyc CPUs and Instinct MI355X GPU accelerators. IBM also has a partnership with Japan's RIKEN scientific research institute under which an IBM Quantum System Two has been integrated with the Fugaku Arm-based supercomputer, once the most powerful system in the world. ®

Gravitational lensing, first predicted by Albert Einstein, occurs when the gravity of a massive foreground object, such as a galaxy or cluster of galaxies, bends, warps, and magnifies the light from a more distant background object. The effect is similar to that of a giant lens in space that allows astronomers to view objects much farther away than any telescope could see on its own. The lenses in this image formed from the precise alignment of a distant background galaxy with the mass of a foreground galaxy, creating distorted and magnified images of the background galaxy that appear as arcs around the foreground galaxy. Lenses like these will be used to investigate the evolution of galaxies and dark matter. Credit: NASA, ESA, and X. Huang (University of San Francisco); Processing: Gladys Kober (NASA/Catholic University of America) A gallery of gravitational lenses captured by NASA’s Hubble Space Telescope showcases the diversity of this cosmic phenomenon and lays the groundwork for follow-up observations by the new Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope. Gravitational lensing, first predicted by Albert Einstein, occurs when the gravity of a massive foreground object, such as a galaxy or cluster of galaxies, bends, warps, and magnifies the light from a more distant background object. The effect is similar to that of a giant lens in space that allows astronomers to view objects much farther away than any telescope could see on its own. The lenses in this image formed from the precise alignment of a distant background galaxy with the mass of a foreground galaxy, creating distorted and magnified images of the background galaxy that appear as arcs around the foreground galaxy. Astronomers will use these observations of a large and varied population of gravitational lenses to construct lens models that will help determine how much mass is in the lensing system’s foreground galaxy – and potentially prove or dispel a theory about dark matter. Astronomers study the amount of distortion of the lensed background galaxies to determine the quantity and distribution of mass in the foreground galaxy, including its invisible dark matter. Hubble views the cosmos primarily in visible and ultraviolet light with some infrared coverage, providing a comprehensive, high-resolution view of individual objects. Roman sees primarily infrared light and some visible, over a much larger field of view to create panoramas of the universe. While Hubble gets a better view of individual lenses, Roman will be able to capture more lenses with its wider field-of-view. If Roman finds a particularly interesting lens, researchers may use Hubble to take follow-up observations using its visible and UV prowess for individual objects. With Hubble’s high-resolution imaging and precise models, researchers should also be able to detect small imperfections in these gravitationally lensed galaxy arcs that would indicate the presence of small clumps of dark matter. Researchers could use these previously undetected clumps to confirm the cold dark matter theory, which predicts the existence of many small dark matter clumps of between a million to a billion solar masses. In contrast, the dark matter halo of our Milky Way galaxy is around 1.3 trillion solar masses. By studying Hubble lens images in detail, researchers intend to build a super-intelligence tool to efficiently search similar arcs in the upcoming Roman images. The Hubble images are expected to both yield their own results on dark matter and pave the way for analysis of Roman’s larger sample of lenses. The unique lenses in this image display some of the different characteristics researchers will see as they collect a diverse and numerous assortment of lenses to test in their models. Panel A is an example of an arc-counterarc configuration, in which the lensed background galaxy appears as a duplicated pair of arcs. The lensed galaxy is being magnified by a pair of foreground galaxies whose combined mass bends the light of the background galaxy around them. The diversity of lenses in this image demonstrate some of the characteristics researchers will uncover with Hubble and Roman. Each lens differs significantly from others in the panel. Credit: NASA, ESA, and X. Huang (University of San Francisco); Processing: Gladys Kober (NASA/Catholic University of America) Panel F is an Einstein Ring, in which the alignment of the background galaxy and approximately spherical mass of the foreground lens are so perfectly situated that the lensed galaxy almost fully encircles the foreground galaxy. Panel I shows a quadruply lensed galaxy, in which the background galaxy is replicated four times, appearing as smeared dots around the foreground galaxy. Panel C also shows a quadruply lensed galaxy, with double knots that are most likely strong star-forming regions in the background galaxy. Some of the magnified and warped background galaxies appear blue and some appear red. These bluish arcs indicate young stars, while reddish arcs indicate older stars. Roman and Hubble will explore these differences to better understand how galaxies evolved earlier in the universe. Most of the foreground lensing galaxies are elliptical galaxies, which are older, denser, and more compact. Lensed images of background galaxies only occur when the mass density of the foreground galaxy reaches a critical point. But not all of these foreground galaxies are ellipticals, and researchers can use these differences to explore the evolutionary paths taken by these galaxies. In panel G, the foreground galaxy appears elongated, which may be true or a trick of perspective, and in panels B and F, the foreground galaxies appear to have spiral arms. Panel D’s foreground galaxy has a visible dust lane, which is rare in a lensing galaxy and the kind of detail that Hubble’s sharp, visible-light vision excels at revealing. The lensed background galaxy could be an Einstein Ring, with the dust lane “breaking” our view of the ring. Because infrared light is less obscured by dust, future Roman infrared observations could help determine whether the arcs form a more complete Einstein ring. These strong lenses were first detected with The Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument at Kitt Peak. Hubble subsequently observed them, and Roman will take further observations. Images like these are an example of the kinds of collaborative efforts that routinely take place between NASA’s Great Observatories to build a comprehensive picture of the cosmos. As Roman joins the family of large space observatories that includes Hubble, the Chandra X-ray Observatory, and the James Webb Space Telescope, a new window opens onto the universe, revealing sights previously hidden while expanding our cosmic knowledge for all of humanity. item.title: Zimbabwean author Simbarashe Kundizeza cleared of using AI to write prize-winning story
item.description: After a month-long investigation it was concluded that Kundizeza’s story The Blue Fighter, which won the £10,000 Caine prize, was ‘human-written’ The Zimbabwean author Simbarashe Kundizeza has been cleared of using AI to write a prize-winning short story, after the prestigious Caine prize for African writers concluded that his entry was “human-written” after a month-long investigation. Kundizeza’s story The Blue Fighter , which charts the declining fortunes of a family after the father invests in fish tanks, was announced as the winner of the £10,000 prize on 6 October. Continue reading...

item.title: 2026 CAF Awards: Date, Venue, Nominees & Everything to Know
item.description: Achraf Hakimi with his trophy after winning African Player of the Year at the 2025 CAF Awards. Photo Credit: CAF/Instagram For the first time in 12 years, Lagos will host the CAF Awards, with the 2026 ceremony scheduled for Wednesday, 2 December. The event, which was originally set for 7 December, will bring together leading African footballers, coaches and teams at the Professor Wole Soyinka Centre for Culture and the Arts in Iganmu. Spanning 18 award categories across men’s and women’s football, the 2026 CAF Awards will celebrate the finest players, coaches, national teams, and clubs across the continent while bringing football royalty, Nollywood stars, Afrobeats performers, and fashion insiders together on one red carpet. The 2026 shortlists come with a notable twist for the host nation. No Nigerian player made the ten-man shortlist for the CAF Men’s Player of the Year award—leaving out Super Eagles stars Victor Osimhen and Ademola Lookman alongside Egypt’s Mohamed Salah —and no Nigerian footballer features in the CAF Women’s Player of the Year category either, with three-time Women’s Goalkeeper of the Year winner Chiamaka Nnadozie also absent from the final lists. Chiamaka Nnadozie celebrating her third consecutive Goalkeeper of the Year win at the 2025 CAF Awards. Photo Credit: Chiamaka Nnadozie/Instagram Even so, Nigeria still has four nominations to look forward to on home soil on 2 December. The Super Falcons are nominated for Women’s National Team of the Year alongside Algeria, Cabo Verde, Cameroon, Côte d’Ivoire, Ghana, Malawi, Mali, Morocco, and South Africa. In the individual women’s categories, Edo Queens and Falconets shot-stopper Christiana Uzoma represents Nigeria on the Women’s Goalkeeper of the Year shortlist, while Nigerian youth internationals Seimeyeha Janet Akekoromowei and Oluwakemi Adegbuyi are both in the running for Women’s Young Player of the Year. Elsewhere, the headline races feature some of the biggest names in global football. Defending winner Achraf Hakimi of Morocco and Paris Saint-Germain leads the CAF Men’s Player of the Year nominees alongside his compatriots Brahim Diaz and Ismael Saibari , Senegal’s Sadio Mané , Ismaila Sarr , and Pape Gueye , Côte d’Ivoire’s Amad Diallo , Ghana’s Antoine Semenyo , DR Congo’s Yoane Wissa , and South Africa’s Teboho Mokoena . Ademola Lookman celebrating his Men’s Player of the Year victory at the 2024 CAF Awards. Photo Credit: Ademola Lookman/Instagram Over in the CAF Women’s Player of the Year race, Zambia’s Barbra Banda and Malawi’s Tabitha and Temwa Chawinga headline a competitive ten-player shortlist that also includes South Africa’s Thembi Kgatlana, Ghana’s Portia Boakye , Algeria’s Marine Dafeur, Morocco’s Hanan Ait El Haj , and Cameroon trio Marie Ngah Manga , Michaely Bihina , and Monique Ngock . Other major honours on the night include Men’s and Women’s Goalkeeper of the Year, Interclub Player of the Year, Coach of the Year, Young Player of the Year, National Team of

item.title: Hackers exploiting ScreenConnect plugin flaw to spread malware across hundreds of PCs
item.description: Hackers have used a dodgy third-party ScreenConnect extension to push malware onto at least 288 machines across 48 organizations, prompting ConnectWise to disable a handful of plugins in hundreds of customer environments. Security outfit Huntress first raised the alarm in a Reddit post on Wednesday, warning of an active campaign targeting cloud-hosted ScreenConnect instances. At the time, its security operations center was tracking six compromised managed service providers (MSPs) and more than 286 affected endpoints, with the numbers still climbing. ConnectWise acquired popular remote supporttool ScreenConnect in February, 2015. Huntress spotted the attacks at around 1747 UTC, when someone began using ScreenConnect's remote command feature to install rogue clients on machines managed by multiple IT service providers. All 288 endpoints were hit within 90 minutes, with roughly a third compromised in the first ten minutes. Huntress suspects more MSPs may have been compromised, as the attackers appeared to be numbering their victims sequentially, with the numbers suggesting earlier attacks that it hadn't detected. The attackers deployed a 16-file malware toolkit dubbed SCKit, which installs a separate ScreenConnect client to maintain remote access even if the legitimate connection is shut down. It also contains code designed to spread the infection to IT technicians and potentially other customers under their control. Huntress has since traced the activity to a possible authentication weakness in RMM+, a third-party extension that lets other management tools issue commands through ScreenConnect without technicians using its console. Versions 1.0.31 and 1.0.32 of the extension contain a flaw that means installations without a configured access key will accept a blank one. Because RMM+ operates independently of ScreenConnect's normal user accounts and authentication controls, an attacker could potentially execute commands without defeating MFA. Huntress said the findings matched what its investigators saw during the attacks, with commands reaching machines across several ScreenConnect installations despite no corresponding login activity. The researchers also confirmed that the attacks affected ScreenConnect versions 26.6.6.9747 and 26.7.6.9783, meaning administrators running the latest releases weren't necessarily safe. ConnectWise has acknowledged that third-party extensions may have been involved but has stopped short of confirming how the attackers initially gained access. In a security advisory , the company said it was investigating unauthorized access to certain partner environments and had identified approximately 400 installations containing at least one extension from the RMM+ family. It has disabled five extensions, including RMM+, RMM Plus, and Labtech Plus, wherever it can do so remotely, and urged customers running their own ScreenConnect servers to follow suit. item.content:encoded: Hackers have used a dodgy third-party ScreenConnect extension to push malware onto at least 288 machines across 48 organizations, prompting ConnectWise to disable a handful of plugins in hundreds of customer environments. Security outfit Huntress first raised the alarm in a Reddit post on Wednesday, warning of an active campaign targeting cloud-hosted ScreenConnect instances. At the time, its security operations center was tracking six compromised managed service providers (MSPs) and more than 286 affected endpoints, with the numbers still climbing. ConnectWise acquired popular remote supporttool ScreenConnect in February, 2015. Huntress spotted the attacks at around 1747 UTC, when someone began using ScreenConnect's remote command feature to install rogue clients on machines managed by multiple IT service providers. All 288 endpoints were hit within 90 minutes, with roughly a third compromised in the first ten minutes. Huntress suspects more MSPs may have been compromised, as the attackers appeared to be numbering their victims sequentially, with the numbers suggesting earlier attacks that it hadn't detected. The attackers deployed a 16-file malware toolkit dubbed SCKit, which installs a separate ScreenConnect client to maintain remote access even if the legitimate connection is shut down. It also contains code designed to spread the infection to IT technicians and potentially other customers under their control. Huntress has since traced the activity to a possible authentication weakness in RMM+, a third-party extension that lets other management tools issue commands through ScreenConnect without technicians using its console. Versions 1.0.31 and 1.0.32 of the extension contain a flaw that means installations without a configured access key will accept a blank one. Because RMM+ operates independently of ScreenConnect's normal user accounts and authentication controls, an attacker could potentially execute commands without defeating MFA. Huntress said the findings matched what its investigators saw during the attacks, with commands reaching machines across several ScreenConnect installations despite no corresponding login activity. The researchers also confirmed that the attacks affected ScreenConnect versions 26.6.6.9747 and 26.7.6.9783, meaning administrators running the latest releases weren't necessarily safe. ConnectWise has acknowledged that third-party extensions may have been involved but has stopped short of confirming how the attackers initially gained access. In a security advisory , the company said it was investigating unauthorized access to certain partner environments and had identified approximately 400 installations containing at least one extension from the RMM+ family. It has disabled five extensions, including RMM+, RMM Plus, and Labtech Plus, wherever it can do so remotely, and urged customers running their own ScreenConnect servers to follow suit. ConnectWise stressed that the 400 environments were identified because they had the extensions installed, not because they were necessarily compromised. The company said: "At this time, we have found no evidence of a compromise of ConnectWise infrastructure or a vulnerability in ScreenConnect itself." There's another nasty trick buried in SCKit. According to Huntress, the malware is designed to turn an infected computer into a trap for the technician sent to investigate it. If the technician connects through ScreenConnect, the toolkit attempts to transfer malware back to their workstation, steal authentication cookies, and use their access to infect other machines. That could give attackers a route from one compromised customer into others managed by the same IT provider. However, Huntress says it has yet to see that part of the attack succeed. "We have not observed that method to spread work successfully. The console-takeover attempt failed in every recovered host log we have checked so far," the researchers wrote. Huntress also suspects that some of the malware's C# code was generated using an LLM, pointing to unusually detailed comments explaining what the code is supposed to do. Apparently, even malware authors appreciate a little help with their homework. Both Huntress and ConnectWise are urging administrators not to investigate suspected infections by remotely connecting through ScreenConnect, since doing so could put the technician's own machine at risk. Administrators are being advised to use other security tools to investigate affected machines, look for rogue ScreenConnect clients, and check what commands have been run. Any malware left behind will also need to be removed before the machines are brought back online. Huntress warned on Reddit that some machines were becoming reinfected within minutes of being taken out of isolation because the malware had not been properly removed. Simply disabling the vulnerable extensions won't necessarily undo the damage, either. As ConnectWise warns, "Disabling extensions and resetting credentials alone may not remove unauthorized software, persistence mechanisms, or access already established on endpoints." And with the attackers already able to install their own remote access software, kicking them out could prove considerably harder than closing the door they came through. ®

item.title: Through NASA’s Lens: Capturing Space Shuttle Endeavour’s Move to LA
item.description: 3 Min Read Through NASA’s Lens: Capturing Space Shuttle Endeavour’s Move to LA A spectacular sight as NASA’s Shuttle Carrier Aircraft with space shuttle Endeavour atop soars over the Golden Gate Bridge. Credits: NASA/Carla Thomas As a new exhibit opens showcasing NASA’s space shuttle Endeavour, NASA photographers look back at the final mission. These photographers documented the iconic images shared around the world on Sept. 21, 2012, while millions watched space shuttle Endeavour fly on top of the agency’s 747 Shuttle Carrier Aircraft for the last time. Endeavour’s new home at the California Science Center in Los Angeles will reopen the weekend of Nov. 13, displayed upright in launch position, ready to inspire the next generation of space explorers. NASA/Lori Losey “Chasing Endeavour’s final ferry flight over Southern California was, without a doubt, a leading highlight of my 37-year career at NASA,” said Lori Losey, lead videographer at NASA’s Armstrong Flight Research Center in Edwards, California. “I advocated for two chase aircraft to be used in the LA area so we could dedicate one aircraft to photo and one to video. It was this beautiful dance of alternating altitudes and swapping positions between landmarks to maximize both of us capturing the legendary imagery.” Two photographers and one videographer, all based at NASA Armstrong, had a leading hand in preparing the Endeavour’s flight to Los Angeles, and in deciding where else the aircraft would fly around California on its final journey. Agency pilots planned the route to fly across some of California’s most iconic landmarks and the imagery team strategized about how to best capture the images. Thousands of visitors to Disneyland and Disney’s California Adventure parks got a special treat when NASA’s Shuttle Carrier Aircraft with space shuttle Endeavour on top flew over at low level during its flyover of Los Angeles. NASA/Jim Ross “The most fun thing about this project was seeing the excitement of the people on the ground as we flew over the different landmarks,” said Jim Ross, NASA Armstrong’s lead photographer. “People in the Los Angeles area really came out and supported the Endeavour flyover. We saw so many supporters at Griffith Park and Disneyland.” Photographer Carla Thomas said seeing the standing-room-only crowd below the California State Capitol in Sacramento filled her with pride. After joining the agency in the wake of the Challenger tragedy, she reflected on the opportunity to document NASA’s return to flight. The space shuttle Endeavour and its 747 carrier aircraft makes a low-level flyover of the Los Angeles Memorial Coliseum. NASA/Jim Ross Endeavour was escorted by NASA Armstrong’s F/A-18s and an F-15, which carried the photo and video teams in the back seats. item.content:encoded: 3 Min Read Through NASA’s Lens: Capturing Space Shuttle Endeavour’s Move to LA A spectacular sight as NASA’s Shuttle Carrier Aircraft with space shuttle Endeavour atop soars over the Golden Gate Bridge. Credits: NASA/Carla Thomas As a new exhibit opens showcasing NASA’s space shuttle Endeavour, NASA photographers look back at the final mission. These photographers documented the iconic images shared around the world on Sept. 21, 2012, while millions watched space shuttle Endeavour fly on top of the agency’s 747 Shuttle Carrier Aircraft for the last time. Endeavour’s new home at the California Science Center in Los Angeles will reopen the weekend of Nov. 13, displayed upright in launch position, ready to inspire the next generation of space explorers. NASA/Lori Losey “Chasing Endeavour’s final ferry flight over Southern California was, without a doubt, a leading highlight of my 37-year career at NASA,” said Lori Losey, lead videographer at NASA’s Armstrong Flight Research Center in Edwards, California. “I advocated for two chase aircraft to be used in the LA area so we could dedicate one aircraft to photo and one to video. It was this beautiful dance of alternating altitudes and swapping positions between landmarks to maximize both of us capturing the legendary imagery.” Two photographers and one videographer, all based at NASA Armstrong, had a leading hand in preparing the Endeavour’s flight to Los Angeles, and in deciding where else the aircraft would fly around California on its final journey. Agency pilots planned the route to fly across some of California’s most iconic landmarks and the imagery team strategized about how to best capture the images. Thousands of visitors to Disneyland and Disney’s California Adventure parks got a special treat when NASA’s Shuttle Carrier Aircraft with space shuttle Endeavour on top flew over at low level during its flyover of Los Angeles. NASA/Jim Ross “The most fun thing about this project was seeing the excitement of the people on the ground as we flew over the different landmarks,” said Jim Ross, NASA Armstrong’s lead photographer. “People in the Los Angeles area really came out and supported the Endeavour flyover. We saw so many supporters at Griffith Park and Disneyland.” Photographer Carla Thomas said seeing the standing-room-only crowd below the California State Capitol in Sacramento filled her with pride. After joining the agency in the wake of the Challenger tragedy, she reflected on the opportunity to document NASA’s return to flight. The space shuttle Endeavour and its 747 carrier aircraft makes a low-level flyover of the Los Angeles Memorial Coliseum. NASA/Jim Ross Endeavour was escorted by NASA Armstrong’s F/A-18s and an F-15, which carried the photo and video teams in the back seats. Like many flight efforts, this journey took a significant amount of preplanning with the California Science Center, as well as groups like the Federal Aviation Administration, the Los Angeles International Airport, and NASA’s Johnson Space Center in Houston. “The planning was my favorite part of this effort — it was fun and exciting to plan the shots,” Thomas said. “I flew the entire route with the LAPD (Los Angeles Police Department) in one of their helicopters. We had to make sure this was going to work and find any obstacles. Planning for the Hollywood sign was challenging, because it’s on the side of a hill with power lines and radio antennas, but we worked through these issues in the planning process.” Space shuttle Endeavour atop its modified 747 carrier aircraft overflies the former Alameda Naval Air Station adjoining San Francisco Bay during the Tour of California. NASA/Carla Thomas The space shuttle’s flight path included other California landmarks: Dodger Stadium, the Getty Center, the Los Angeles Memorial Coliseum, NASA’s Ames Research Center in Silicon Valley, the Golden Gate Bridge, NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Pasadena, and the Santa Monica Pier. Endeavour helped begin assembly of the International Space Station by delivering its first components to orbit and went on to complete 25 missions. The space shuttle will soon be seen, along with some of the images from the final flight, in its permanent home inside the new Samuel Oschin Air and Space Center at the California Science Center in Downtown Los Angeles. Shuttle Endeavour was ferried to Los Angeles, briefly flying over the California state capitol, Sacramento, then demated from its NASA 747 and trailered to the California Science Center. item.title: Astronomers stunned after James Webb Space Telescope discovers the earliest pair of black hole-powered quasars
item.description: null Using the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST), astronomers have discovered the oldest pair of supermassive black hole-powered quasars ever seen. There's just one problem: they shouldn't exist! The compact quasar pair, spotted with the aid of the Gemini North telescope, has been designated J1602+4228AB and nicknamed Nāpōwawāʻenakaulua, which means "Two celestial bodies of fathomless powerful darkness in the brilliance of heat reincarnating energy into the universe." The compact quasar pair is seen as it was 900 million years after the Big Bang at a time when such supermassive black holes should not have had time to grow to such tremendous masses. Nāpōwawāʻenakaulua isn't just the oldest and most distant quasar pairing ever seen. There is just 18,100 light-years, or roughly one-fifth the diameter of the Milky Way, between the supermassive black holes, which have masses of 1.5 billion and 400 million times that of the sun. That makes Nāpōwawāʻenakaulua the most compact quasar pair found during a period of the universe's history known as Cosmic Dawn , shortly after the birth of the first stars, galaxies, and black holes. "There is no definitive theoretical explanation for how a single one of these giant quasars exists so early in the age of our universe, much less two," research team leader Silvia Onorato of the NOIRLab said in a statement . "We observed Nāpōwawāʻenakaulua at a time when the universe was only a thirteenth of its age and, astonishingly, its supermassive black holes are just as massive as those we see today." How were supermassive black holes over fed at Cosmic Dawn Quasars occur when the supermassive black holes that sit at the heart of large galaxies are surrounded by a flattened cloud of swirling gas and dust called an "accretion disk," from which they feed or "accrete" matter. The immense gravity of the central black hole causes friction, heating the accretion disk and causing it to glow, often brighter than the combined light of every star in the surrounding galaxy. We see that glow as a quasar. Finding such objects in the recent cosmic history of the 13.8-billion-year-old universe isn't troubling, though finding compact pairs of them is still extremely rare. Such pairs should be common because the merger of galaxies that brings together supermassive black holes is frequent. That should lead to an abundance of pairs of quasars with a separation less than the typical size of a galaxy. There are three reasons this has proven tricky. Firstly, the "quasar phase" of a supermassive black hole is relatively short on cosmic terms. Secondly, even relatively close quasar pairs are very far away, making them faint and hard to detect with ground-based telescopes. Finally, at such great distances and with such a small separation between the two supermassive black holes, the individual members of a quasar pair are hard to individually resolve. Such pairs should be common because the merger of galaxies that brings together supermassive black holes is frequent. That should lead to an abundance of pairs of quasars with a separation less than the typical size of a galaxy. There are three reasons this has proven tricky. Firstly, the "quasar phase" of a supermassive black hole is relatively short on cosmic terms. Secondly, even relatively close quasar pairs are very far away, making them faint and hard to detect with ground-based telescopes. Finally, at such great distances and with such a small separation between the two supermassive black holes, the individual members of a quasar pair are hard to individually resolve. Yet, astronomers do find quasar pairs. Sometimes at distances and times that they would probably rather not, because it challenges everything we know about black hole growth. An annotated illustration of Nāpōwawāʻenakaulua showing its place in cosmic history. (Image credit: International Gemini Observatory/NOIRLab/NSF/AURA/P. Marenfeld/M. Zamani) The trouble arises before the universe was 1 billion years. That is because, according to current models, black holes should need at least 1 billion years to feed and merge enough to reach masses millions or billions of times that of the sun. Yet, since it began operations in 2022, the JWST has been routinely discovering supermassive black holes powering quasars as early as 400 million years after the Big Bang. If that wasn't confusing enough, the discovery of Nāpōwawāʻenakaulua, the third quasar pair seen at Cosmic Dawn, could really break current models. Nāpōwawāʻenakaulua was uncovered in data from the JWST's Aether survey, which is conducting a census of objects in the early universe. Using JWST’s NIRSpec (Near-Infrared Spectrograph Integral Field Unit) instrument, the survey has uncovered 200 quasars, just under half of all currently known early universe quasars. It was while browsing the Aether dataset that the team discovered that quasar J1602+4228A is not alone, it had a companion now designated J1602+4228B. Resolving these two quasars should have been nearly impossible from the ground. But this was possible for Gemini North thanks to perfect timing and perfect weather conditions over Maunakea , the dormant volcano on the island of Hawai'i where the telescope is located. A definite scientific feat, Nāpōwawāʻenakaulua remains a mystery for now, but it could actually help scientists better understand how galaxies were coming together during Cosmic Dawn, a vital stage in the evolution of the universe. "Nāpōwawāʻenakaulua is a really unique environment," Onorato said. "It's a laboratory for astronomers to study how the very first massive galaxies and their central black holes assembled together through direct galaxy interactions during these early times." The team's results were published on Tuesday (Nov. 10) The Astrophysical Journal Letters.

item.title: Celebrating 50 Years of Nourishment: Maltina Introduces Its New Look to Trade Partners
item.description: Maltina has unveiled its refreshed visual identity at a trade launch event in Lagos, marking 50 years of nourishing Nigerian homes and introducing a new look for the iconic malt brand while retaining the taste and nutritional qualities consumers have come to love. Held on Friday, November 6, 2026, at the Balmoral Convention Centre, Ikeja, the event brought together business partners, distributors, consumers and other distinguished guests to celebrate the milestone and experience the refreshed brand through interactive activities, entertainment and product showcases. First introduced as Maltona in 1976 and renamed Maltina in 1977, the brand has maintained a strong presence in Nigerian homes for over five decades. Its journey has been defined by a commitment to nourishment, including its introduction of multivitamin enrichment in 1993 and calcium fortification in 2009. Beyond its product innovations, Maltina continues to build meaningful connections with consumers through initiatives such as Maltina Nourishment Tour, Maltina Dance All, Maltina Teacher of the Year (MTOTY), and its Christmas and Ramadan festive campaigns, creating opportunities for learning, participation and shared experiences. Speaking at the event, Sarah Agha , Marketing Director, Nigerian Breweries Plc., reflected on the brand’s journey and the thinking behind its refreshed identity. She highlighted Maltina’s longstanding commitment to nourishment and happiness, noting that the new look represents a more contemporary and confident expression of the brand as it prepares for its next chapter. The refreshed packaging features an enriched signature orange, gold accents and barley elements that reinforce Maltina’s malt credentials. The updated sunrays represent vitality and optimism, while the more prominent calcium coin highlights its nourishment proposition. The gold crown cork and the addition of ‘Since 1976’ further celebrate the brand’s heritage. She reassured consumers that while the brand’s visual identity has evolved, its familiar taste and nutritional credentials remain unchanged. She said “This is not just about refreshing our identity; it is about reaffirming our commitment to nourishment and to families across Nigeria. Our new look makes these commitments even more visible. While our identity has evolved to welcome a new chapter, our taste and nutritional credentials remain unchanged. It is still New Look, Same Nourishing Taste,” In his welcome address, Thibaut Boidin , Managing Director, Nigerian Breweries Plc., celebrated Maltina’s remarkable journey and acknowledged the consumers, partners and distributors whose continued support has contributed to the brand’s growth. He also reiterated the company’s commitment to social impact, announcing plans to support the education of children from underserved communities in the coming year. item.title: The latest FreeBSD report is here, and the AI debate is ongoing
item.description: The FreeBSD project's status team has published FreeBSD's third status report of 2026, showing plenty of ambitious work underway and a community still undecided on how to treat code from AI coding assistants. The FreeBSD Status Report Third Quarter 2026 is a substantial document, with 51 entries from five teams covering 16 projects, plus six other sections with more detailed reports. There are updates on the progress of the Sylve project, which is an attempt to bring a smooth polished GUI for managing FreeBSD virtualization hosts – something akin to Proxmox for FreeBSD. We mentioned this when we looked at the new Daemonarchy project last month. Another covers the new AppJail effort – a containerized app distribution system for FreeBSD, including for GUI apps, which aims for something broadly comparable to Snap, Flatpak and AppImage on Linux. In other words, interesting and quite radical stuff is happening in the FreeBSD space. What this particular LLM-skeptical vulture was most interested to see, though, was an update on the internal discussion about how to handle code generated by AI coding assistants in the project. We first reported on this vexed subject back in September 2025 and no final answer has yet been published. NetBSD banned AI-generated code in 2024 and although the bot-boosters say this will doom it to irrelevance, as we reported last month, the project is thriving . Also back in October, we looked at OpenBSD 8.0 , whose launch materials are full of mockery for AI users. Under the FreeBSD Core Team section , there is a subsection headed "FreeBSD Developer AI survey." The survey was created by Baptiste Daroussin, and received 140 responses. Although the percentages show that there is some resistance to AI, there are hints here as to why it’s taking so long. Some project committers are against it, yet many more are proponents. Since there are only seven bullet points, we thought we would quote them in full: Policy: 88 percent want the Project to adopt a policy, either a formal, written policy (49 percent ) or light guidance and best practices (39 percent ). Six percent said that AI should be explicitly discouraged, and three percent that the existing contribution rules are sufficient. AI-assisted code: 35 percent said it must be disclosed, 25 percent that it must be reviewed more strictly than human code, 22 percent that it should be treated like any other contribution, and 16 percent that it should be rejected outright. Safeguards: mandatory human review (78 percent ) and mandatory disclosure (69 percent ) were requested most often, followed by provenance or licensing documentation (47 percent ) and mandatory testing (39 percent ). Disclosure: 84 percent want AI use disclosed, either always (48 percent ) or when its involvement is significant (36 percent ). 79 percent want AI-assisted commits marked in the commit log, and 56 percent prefer a tag that names the tool. Concerns: the main concerns about quality are correctness and subtle
item.dc:creator: Liam Proven
item.content:encoded: The FreeBSD project's status team has published FreeBSD's third status report of 2026, showing plenty of ambitious work underway and a community still undecided on how to treat code from AI coding assistants. The FreeBSD Status Report Third Quarter 2026 is a substantial document, with 51 entries from five teams covering 16 projects, plus six other sections with more detailed reports. There are updates on the progress of the Sylve project, which is an attempt to bring a smooth polished GUI for managing FreeBSD virtualization hosts – something akin to Proxmox for FreeBSD. We mentioned this when we looked at the new Daemonarchy project last month. Another covers the new AppJail effort – a containerized app distribution system for FreeBSD, including for GUI apps, which aims for something broadly comparable to Snap, Flatpak and AppImage on Linux. In other words, interesting and quite radical stuff is happening in the FreeBSD space. What this particular LLM-skeptical vulture was most interested to see, though, was an update on the internal discussion about how to handle code generated by AI coding assistants in the project. We first reported on this vexed subject back in September 2025 and no final answer has yet been published. NetBSD banned AI-generated code in 2024 and although the bot-boosters say this will doom it to irrelevance, as we reported last month, the project is thriving . Also back in October, we looked at OpenBSD 8.0 , whose launch materials are full of mockery for AI users. Under the FreeBSD Core Team section , there is a subsection headed "FreeBSD Developer AI survey." The survey was created by Baptiste Daroussin, and received 140 responses. Although the percentages show that there is some resistance to AI, there are hints here as to why it’s taking so long. Some project committers are against it, yet many more are proponents. Since there are only seven bullet points, we thought we would quote them in full: Policy: 88 percent want the Project to adopt a policy, either a formal, written policy (49 percent ) or light guidance and best practices (39 percent ). Six percent said that AI should be explicitly discouraged, and three percent that the existing contribution rules are sufficient. AI-assisted code: 35 percent said it must be disclosed, 25 percent that it must be reviewed more strictly than human code, 22 percent that it should be treated like any other contribution, and 16 percent that it should be rejected outright. Safeguards: mandatory human review (78 percent ) and mandatory disclosure (69 percent ) were requested most often, followed by provenance or licensing documentation (47 percent ) and mandatory testing (39 percent ). Disclosure: 84 percent want AI use disclosed, either always (48 percent ) or when its involvement is significant (36 percent ). 79 percent want AI-assisted commits marked in the commit log, and 56 percent prefer a tag that names the tool. Concerns: the main concerns about quality are correctness and subtle bugs (39 percent , licensing and provenance (26 percent ), and maintainability (21 percent ). 75 percent are somewhat or very concerned about copyright and licensing. Principles: accountability, meaning that a human remains responsible (91 percent ), and transparency (78 percent ) were selected most often, and preserving code quality was the top-ranked goal for a policy. Other uses: 65 percent would allow AI-generated documentation with human review. 54 percent would allow AI tools on Project infrastructure, most of them with restrictions, and 29 percent would not. Only six percent for explicit discouragement, 16 percent for outright rejection, and 35 percent against LLM-generated documentation. This plus the usual sort of calls for responsible use and disclosure, concerns about copyright issues, and so on. The Reg is strongly reminded of the Debian developer poll we reported on in August . This had no fewer than four slightly different AI-refusal options out of eight, and despite the Condorcet voting method it uses, the result was giving permission to use bots . With such relatively weak opposition, we suspect that FreeBSD will go the same way as Debian: tell developers to be careful, but allow bot usage, resulting in LLM-extruded code being committed into the project. ®

item.title: Microsoft admits SQL Servers might wobble after October update
item.description: Encountered some odd SQL Server connection behavior since the October update? There might be a culprit… Microsoft has admitted that a change has caused linked server queries to fail to close connections. Linked servers via OLE DB providers have been around for years and are a useful way of, for example, using additional data sources in queries. Once a provider is added, SQL Server can open a connection to grab data, and close it again when the query is complete. Or, at least, that's the theory. The problem is that after the October 13 (KB5126646) update, connections created by SQL Server linked server queries might remain open. According to Microsoft, "As additional queries are performed, connections to external databases can accumulate instead of closing as expected. "This can slow or degrade server performance after prolonged run time." You think? Administrators will likely have already noted a suspicious number of open connections to external databases on affected systems. Microsoft said the issue affects SQL Server linked server queries that use OLE DB providers to connect to external databases. It gave PostgreSQL and Oracle as examples of connections known to be affected. And the fix? "If idle connections can be identified, it is possible to manually close them to temporarily relieve server load. "It is also possible to temporarily restore system stability by restarting the SQL service." The Windows behemoth went on to state the obvious: "However, these steps can also interrupt active queries or transactions, and the problem can resurface again after sufficient operation time." Bouncing a SQL Server to deal with connection leakage is less than ideal, although it would at least be a good failover test and, let's face it, having to restart Microsoft services regularly is something many administrators will be all too familiar with. There is a mitigation available, although only through Microsoft support for business. Otherwise, an out-of-band update should be along within the next few days to deal with the problem. According to Microsoft, the technical glitch affects every version of Windows except Windows 11 26H2, stretching back to Windows 10 1809 and LTSC 2019, and Windows Server from 2025 back to 2012. Microsoft, or rather the unfortunate souls responsible for administering their server products, has not had the best time of late. The October 2026 Windows Server update left some Exchange Servers wobbling until either a Registry edit was made or a fix was applied as part of the November update. ®

item.title: Michael Carrick was just the latest fall guy for Manchester United’s dysfunctional hierarchy | Jamie Jackson
item.description: Disastrous decisions and confused appointments have been a constant theme at Old Trafford since Sir Alex Ferguson’s retirement in 2013 For a window into the alarming dysfunction at Manchester United that Michael Carrick failed to manage and caused his sacking , consider the case of Eddie Howe, initially a favourite to succeed the 45-year-old before Mauricio Pochettino’s emergence as the chosen one. The former Newcastle manager had been Jason Wilcox’s choice to take over from Carrick. Howe was also the favoured candidate of Dan Ashworth, Wilcox’s predecessor as United’s director of football, to follow Erik ten Hag after the Dutchman’s sacking in October 2024. Except Wilcox disagreed and Sir Jim Ratcliffe went with Wilcox’s man, Ruben Amorim, and that December Ashworth departed only five months after joining. Continue reading...

item.title: ‘Pregnancy does not mean game over’: meet the footballers challenging the myths | Moving the Goalposts
item.description: Claire Emslie and Emma Kelly are among those taking advantage of new research and guidelines for pregnant players Claire Emslie wasn’t expecting to be able to run at 81% of her max speed at 32 weeks pregnant. Emslie, a Scotland international who also plays as a forward for Angel City FC , documented her journey through pregnancy and football training on social media and is part of a growing number of professional female footballers who are getting pregnant in their athletic prime and approaching motherhood with a fresh mindset. Rather than marking the end of a career (notably, Millie Bright announced her pregnancy in September, months after having retired), pregnancy can mark both a continuation and a renewal. Continue reading...

item.title: How to Style a Pink Buba With a Mini Skirt: Alex Unusual’s Loving Itohan Look
item.description: Alex Unusual’s gold grillz, crystal floral choker, and cherub-accented sunglasses. Who says a buba has to be paired with a wrapper? Nigerian actress, media personality, and reality television star Asogwa Alexandra A —popularly known as Alex Unusua l—is giving us another way to wear the traditional Yoruba top, and her look for the premiere of Loving Itohan makes a strong case for pairing it with a mini skirt. The actress chose a bright fuchsia satin buba with wide half-sleeves, styling it with a fitted mini skirt made from emerald-green and magenta floral brocade damask . It’s an interesting way to rethink the familiar iro and bubacombination: keep the traditional top, swap the wrapper for a shorter skirt, and let the difference in fabric and colour give the outfit its character. The smooth finish of the pink satin against the patterned damask also shows how to wear two statement fabrics without making them compete . The trick is to give each piece a clear role, with the pink buba providing a bold block of colour and the brocade bringing in pattern and texture. Alex Unusual puts a modern spin on the Yoruba iro and buba with a satin top and brocade mini skirt. The mini skirt also gives the outfit a contemporary take on the Oleku silhouette, which traditionally pairs a loose or fitted buba with a wrapper tied above the knee. Alex’s version plays with that familiar proportion, using a fitted damask skirt in place of the wrapper. If you are wondering how to wear a buba and mini skirt without the proportions feeling off, the secret is balancing volume with structure. Because a traditional buba comes with a relaxed cut and wide sleeves, tucking it cleanly into a fitted, high-waisted mini skirt defines the waist and keeps the silhouette neat rather than boxy. Mixing textures intentionally helps too—pairing a plain silk, satin, or AsoOke top with a patterned damask, jacquard, or beaded mini skirt lets both pieces complement each other rather than clash. Alex Unusual in her contemporary Yoruba buba and mini skirt outfit for the Loving Itohan premiere. She carried the damask into her gele, which was wrapped high into voluminous, sculptural folds. An oversized gold lip-shaped brooch secured one side, adding another detail to the headpiece. Using the same fabric for the skirt and gele also helped bring the different parts of the outfit together, while keeping the pink buba at the centre of the colour story. It’s a styling idea worth borrowing if you’re working with patterned damask and want your accessories to feel connected to the rest of your outfit. Alex Unusual pairs her damask gele with cherub-detailed sunglasses, layered gold jewellery, and custom grillz. Alex’s jewellery and accessories added even more detail. For anyone styling a pink buba, Alex’s choice of accessories offers another useful idea: bring in a second colour from the outfit through your shoes or bag, then use metallic jewellery to tie everything together. She kept her beauty look relatively understated, with defined brows, soft neutral eyeshadow, a hint of emerald liner, and glossy nude lips. item.title: European tech buyers add digital sovereignty to cyber shopping list
item.description: European tech buyers are increasingly choosing cybersecurity vendors from their own continent in a bid to reduce their reliance on American technology. Digital sovereignty isn't only prompting enterprise customers to question their clouds of choice, it is also reshaping other parts of the industry too, and the shift is marked. According to sales figures compiled by Context, distributor sales in EMEA of cybersecurity products from EU-headquartered vendors jumped 35 percent in the two years to calendar Q3 2026. Total cybersecurity sales grew up 10 percent over the same period, and sales by US-run companies went up just 8 percent. That growth is from a relatively small base, though EU vendors gained nearly three percentage points to reach 15 percent of tracked sales by value. There is still a long way to go as US-headquartered vendors accounted for 62 percent. The trend coincides with a loss of trust in the Trump administration among customers outside of America, after it cosied up to autocratic rulers while criticizing and punishing allies with tariffs and more. Context stopped short of assigning blame. It said organizations are reviewing their reliance on third-party tech in light of EU compliance regimes: the NIS2 Directive and Digital Operational Resilience Act (DORA). NIS2, transposed into national law in October 2024 , requires organizations in the bloc to raise their common level of security in the face of digital threats and risks to critical infrastructure. DORA, introduced in January last year, is designed to strengthen cyber security in the financial sector. "Digital sovereignty is becoming a buying decision. As customers and resellers get clearer about what it means in practice, they're asking who holds the encryption keys, who can access sensitive logs and where that data is stored," said Context veep of research Joe Turner. "We're seeing a measurable shift in the EMEA channel. EU vendors gained nearly three points of sales share in two years. An organization can keep its existing identity platform and still choose a European supplier to manage its security logs. That's the kind of decision that gives European vendors an opening." The stats indicate that EU-HQd vendors comprised 92 percent of tracked sales in security awareness training, 82 percent in vulnerability management, and 52 percent for SIEM and log management. US-headquartered companies held into 74 percent of identity and access management sales and 54 percent of cloud security sales. item.dc:creator: Paul Kunert
item.content:encoded: European tech buyers are increasingly choosing cybersecurity vendors from their own continent in a bid to reduce their reliance on American technology. Digital sovereignty isn't only prompting enterprise customers to question their clouds of choice, it is also reshaping other parts of the industry too, and the shift is marked. According to sales figures compiled by Context, distributor sales in EMEA of cybersecurity products from EU-headquartered vendors jumped 35 percent in the two years to calendar Q3 2026. Total cybersecurity sales grew up 10 percent over the same period, and sales by US-run companies went up just 8 percent. That growth is from a relatively small base, though EU vendors gained nearly three percentage points to reach 15 percent of tracked sales by value. There is still a long way to go as US-headquartered vendors accounted for 62 percent. The trend coincides with a loss of trust in the Trump administration among customers outside of America, after it cosied up to autocratic rulers while criticizing and punishing allies with tariffs and more. Context stopped short of assigning blame. It said organizations are reviewing their reliance on third-party tech in light of EU compliance regimes: the NIS2 Directive and Digital Operational Resilience Act (DORA). NIS2, transposed into national law in October 2024 , requires organizations in the bloc to raise their common level of security in the face of digital threats and risks to critical infrastructure. DORA, introduced in January last year, is designed to strengthen cyber security in the financial sector. "Digital sovereignty is becoming a buying decision. As customers and resellers get clearer about what it means in practice, they're asking who holds the encryption keys, who can access sensitive logs and where that data is stored," said Context veep of research Joe Turner. "We're seeing a measurable shift in the EMEA channel. EU vendors gained nearly three points of sales share in two years. An organization can keep its existing identity platform and still choose a European supplier to manage its security logs. That's the kind of decision that gives European vendors an opening." The stats indicate that EU-HQd vendors comprised 92 percent of tracked sales in security awareness training, 82 percent in vulnerability management, and 52 percent for SIEM and log management. US-headquartered companies held into 74 percent of identity and access management sales and 54 percent of cloud security sales. The Reg has asked Context for UK-specific figures to see whether British customers are also voting with their wallets for European alternatives. That certainly isn’t the case for tech purchases in the British public sector, despite Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s professed desire to buy British. Data released yesterday by the Institute for Public Policy Research showed just £1 in every £6 spent by government with the biggest technology suppliers goes to Brit businesses. Still, Burnham only came to power in July so there is time yet for him to put his money where his mouth is. Sovereign AI is another area of concern for enterprise customers. Analyst Omdia said last month that despite the marketing adjective meaning "local assets," almost a third AI providers disclose no proof of sovereignty, and some "expect enterprise to pay for audits to verify their claims." Omdia also found that 80 percent of contracts say network resilience is "out of providers control or responsibility," and "US-headquartered AI providers offer better service transparency and contract terms than a majority of local sovereign AI providers, with providers in India a notable exception." Sovereign services in Omdia's classification include data residency, operational autonomy, jurisdictional sovereignty, and technological autonomy. "Local hosting is not sovereignty. Serious providers must demonstrate their credibility through transparent operations, fair contracts and proof of competence. That includes the network, because data in transit must be sovereign too," said Camille Mendler, research director for telco B2B at Omdia. Someone should tell Microsoft and Anthropic . ®

item.title: Rockstar workers vote on union recognition as GTA VI launch looms
item.description: More than 1,600 Rockstar Games employees in the UK will begin voting on union recognition on Thursday, with the ballot kicking off just a week before the long-awaited launch of Grand Theft Auto VI. The ballot, which opens on November 12 and runs until November 26, will determine whether Rockstar formally recognizes the Rockstar Game Workers Union, part of the Independent Workers Union of Great Britain (IWGB). Nearly all UK employees below director level are eligible to vote. If successful, the union would become the largest recognized union in the UK games industry, giving workers a collective voice. The proposed recognition agreement follows four months of negotiations between Rockstar management and employees. It would allow workers to negotiate over pay, overtime, pensions, bonuses, leave and other employment conditions, while securing consultation rights over HR policies and AI. The vote comes at a particularly busy time for Rockstar, with GTA VI finally due to arrive on November 19, more than 13 years after its predecessor. The game is expected to be one of the biggest entertainment launches in history, although the people responsible for making it have rather more immediate concerns than sales records. "I am incredibly proud of the work we've put into making this game. I'm also proud of the union we've built here. For me, those two things are connected," said Nestor Uriate, an animation programmer and Rockstar Game Workers Union representative. "We care deeply about the games we make, and we want to make sure we can continue doing that work in an environment where we're respected, have a meaningful say over our conditions and can feel secure about our futures." The vote follows a year of bad blood between Rockstar and the IWGB. The union accused the GTA developer of union busting after it fired 31 members in October 2025, claiming they had been singled out for taking part in a private Discord group. Rockstar denied the allegations, insisting the workers were dismissed for gross misconduct rather than their union activities. The dispute subsequently reached an employment tribunal, where Rockstar unsuccessfully attempted to have blacklisting allegations struck from the case . Closing submissions are expected on November 17 and 18, meaning the legal proceedings will reach their final stages just as GTA VI prepares to hit shelves. Despite the ongoing dispute, Rockstar's head of publishing, Jennifer Kolbe, recently indicated that management would respect the outcome of the recognition vote, telling Bloomberg : "We go where the team goes. So if they want a union, they will have a union." The union campaign has also attracted support from elsewhere in the games industry, including SAG-AFTRA and the Communications Workers of America (CWA), which represents workers at Blizzard. Alex Marshall, president of the IWGB, said the vote was an opportunity for Rockstar employees to take greater control over their working conditions. "What happens at Rockstar

The game is expected to be one of the biggest entertainment launches in history, although the people responsible for making it have rather more immediate concerns than sales records. "I am incredibly proud of the work we've put into making this game. I'm also proud of the union we've built here. For me, those two things are connected," said Nestor Uriate, an animation programmer and Rockstar Game Workers Union representative. "We care deeply about the games we make, and we want to make sure we can continue doing that work in an environment where we're respected, have a meaningful say over our conditions and can feel secure about our futures." The vote follows a year of bad blood between Rockstar and the IWGB. The union accused the GTA developer of union busting after it fired 31 members in October 2025, claiming they had been singled out for taking part in a private Discord group. Rockstar denied the allegations, insisting the workers were dismissed for gross misconduct rather than their union activities. Closing submissions are expected on November 17 and 18, meaning the legal proceedings will reach their final stages just as GTA VI prepares to hit shelves. Alex Marshall, president of the IWGB, said the vote was an opportunity for Rockstar employees to take greater control over their working conditions. "What happens at Rockstar matters beyond the studio. Workers across the games industry are watching, and this ballot is an opportunity to show what can be achieved when people come together, organize and build the collective power to shape their own working lives." For Rockstar, November was already shaping up to be a big month. By the time GTA VI has been in players' hands for a week, the company should also know whether its UK workforce has voted to secure a formal seat at the negotiating table. ®

item.title: ‘Second ball’ may be a Sunday league mantra but Yates showed its top-flight relevance
item.description: Midfielder’s old-school attributes came to the fore during Nottingham Forest’s win against Manchester City Modern football is more systematised and data-driven than ever but some things never change. Winning the first ball is important but the second ball – the holy grail for Sunday league footballers – is often more so. Nottingham Forest’s 3-1 win against Manchester City last weekend featured a classic example. Forest led 2-1 inside the last 20 minutes but City, lifted by Rayan Cherki’s sweet half-volley, were pushing for an equaliser. Continue reading...

item.title: NHS England deletes ‘misleading’ claim 137 trusts benefiting from Palantir AI tools
item.description: Exclusive: The Guardian revealed 29 hospital trusts were not or hardly using the controversial patient data tech NHS England has deleted a claim from its website stating 137 hospital trusts are benefiting from Palantir’s AI health data system after the Guardian revealed 29 of them were not using all or most of the controversial technology. Health bosses had published a list of all the NHS bodies “live” with and “realising benefits” from the AI-powered federated data platform (FDP), a system set up to improve patient outcomes, boost operating theatre efficiency and speed up bed discharges. But after 29 trusts said it was either not live or they were not using any of its applications, the original list of hospitals appears to have been taken down. Continue reading...

item.title: Datacentres are deeply unpopular. Has Sweden made one we can all love?
item.description: It is built of wood, resembles an Ikea and its power is totally renewable. Plus, it was built with the local community in mind. Is this facility in Falun the best datacentre in the world? ‘It was pretty cool, when they were building it. It looked like a very large Ikea,” says John Wernvik, of EcoDataCenter. He is giving me a tour of their facility in Falun, Sweden, which could lay claim to being the world’s greenest datacentre – although to many, that is a contradiction in terms. One difference is immediately visible: this datacentre is made out of wood. Huge panels of cross-laminated timber arrived at the site pre-cut, and were assembled by crane according to instructions, like flatpack furniture. Aesthetically, this section of the datacentre is more like an Ikea before the fit-out, a cavernous, echoey, immaculately clean hangar. The wood is not EcoDataCenter’s only claim to sustainability; it is more than just cosmetic, says Wernvik, the company’s chief external relations and sustainability officer. “Compared with a traditional datacentre built with steel and concrete, we lower the embodied carbon of the full structure by three times.” With a complex the size of a football pitch, that is a lot of wood, but, says Wernvik, “the amount of timber one of our datacentres uses takes the Swedish forest about 10 to 15 minutes to grow back”. Continue reading...
